arXiv:1501.02860v3 [math.DS] 23 Sep 2026

Toric Differential Inclusions and
a Proof of the Global Attractor Conjecture

Gheorghe Craciun Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Affiliation: Department of Biomolecular Chemistry Affiliation: University of Wisconsin-Madison Affiliation: e-mail: craciun@math.wisc.edu Affiliation: version 3.0
September 23, 2026
Abstract

The global attractor conjecture says that toric dynamical systems have a globally attracting point (up to linear conservation relations) — or, equivalently, complex balanced systems have a globally attracting point within each stoichiometric compatibility class. A proof of this conjecture implies that a large class of nonlinear dynamical systems on the positive orthant have very simple and stable dynamics. The conjecture originates from the 1972 breakthrough work by Fritz Horn and Roy Jackson, and was formulated in its current form by Horn in 1974.

Toric dynamical systems can be embedded into toric differential inclusions. We show that each bounded positive solution of a toric differential inclusion is contained in an invariant region that prevents it from approaching the boundary of the positive orthant. We use this result to prove the global attractor conjecture. In particular, it follows that all detailed balanced mass action systems and all deficiency zero weakly reversible systems have the global attractor property.

1 Introduction

Any autonomous polynomial dynamical system11 1 or more generally any power law system [3], since we do not assume that the coordinates of the vertex points yy are either integer or non-negative. In particular, if vertex points have non-negative integer coordinates we obtain mass-action systems. on the strictly positive orthant ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0} can be represented as

d​xd​t=∑y→y′∈Gky→y′​xy​(y′−y)\frac{dx}{dt}=\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}\in G}k_{y\to y^{\prime}}x^{y}(y^{\prime}-y) (1)

for some Euclidean embedded graph22 2 A Euclidean embedded graph GG is a finite directed graph whose set of vertices is Y⊂ℝnY\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. See Fig. 1 for examples. GG and some positive constants ky→y′k_{y\to y^{\prime}}, one for each edge33 3 Inspired by notation from reaction networks, we denote an directed edge from yy to y′y^{\prime} by y→y′y\to y^{\prime}. Moreover, if y→y′y\to y^{\prime} is an edge in GG we simply write y→y′∈Gy\to y^{\prime}\in G. y→y′y\to y^{\prime} of GG. (Here xyx^{y} denotes the monomial ∏i=1nxiyi\prod_{i=1}^{n}{x_{i}}^{y_{i}}.) Similarly, any non-autonomous polynomial dynamical system on ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0} can be represented as

d​xd​t=∑y→y′∈Gky→y′​(t)​xy​(y′−y)\frac{dx}{dt}=\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}\in G}k_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t)x^{y}(y^{\prime}-y) (2)

for some nonnegative scalar functions ky→y′​(t)k_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t).

Positive trajectories of (1) and (2) are also trajectories of mass-action systems [16]. There is great interest in understanding the persistence and global stability properties of such dynamical systems [16, 17, 11, 12, 14, 13, 21, 22, 28, 23, 24, 25, 8, 10, 4, 20, 5, 7, 19, 3, 9, 18]. A natural question is the following: for which systems (1) or (2) is it true that trajectories that start in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0} stay away44 4 i.e., for a trajectory x⁡(t)x(t), we have lim inft→∞xi​(t)>0\displaystyle\liminf_{t\to\infty}x_{i}(t)>0 for all i=1,…,ni=1,...,n. Then we say that the trajectory x⁡(t)x(t) is persistent. from the boundary of ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0}?

Given a polynomial dynamical system, the choice of graph GG above is not unique. We will see that if the graph GG can be chosen such that each edge of GG is contained in a cycle55 5 or, equivalently, each connected component of GG is strongly connected. If this is the case, we will say that the graph GG is weakly reversible. , then any bounded trajectory of (1) must be persistent in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0}. More generally, this is also true for solutions of (2), provided that the nonnegative scalar functions ky→y′​(t)k_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t) are bounded away from zero and infinity66 6 i.e., there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that ky→y′​(t)∈[ε,1ε]k_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t)\in[\varepsilon,\frac{1}{\varepsilon}] for all tt. .

In this paper we prove the results mentioned above, and use them to prove the global attractor conjecture, which says that toric dynamical systems have a global attractor within any linear invariant subspace77 7 A linear invariant subspace of (1) is an invariant set 𝒮0=(x0+S0)∩ℝ>0n\mathcal{S}_{0}=(x_{0}+S_{0})\cap\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}, where S0S_{0} is a linear subset of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. For toric dynamical systems we will see that S0=s​p​a​n​{y′−y:y→y′∈G}S_{0}=span\{y^{\prime}-y:y\to y^{\prime}\in G\} gives rise to a linear invariant subspace for any x0∈ℝ>0nx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}. . A toric dynamical system is a polynomial dynamical system88 8 or more generally a power law system [3]. for which there exists a representation of the form (1) that admits a vertex-balanced equilibrium in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0}, i.e., there exists x0∈ℝ>0nx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0} such that for each vertex y¯∈Y\overline{y}\in Y we have

∑y→y¯∈Gky→y¯​x0y=∑y¯→y∈Gky¯→y​x0y¯.\sum_{y\to\overline{y}\in G}k_{y\to\overline{y}}x_{0}^{y}=\sum_{\overline{y}\to y\in G}k_{\overline{y}\to y}x_{0}^{\overline{y}}. (3)

In other words, if we think of the positive number ky→y′​xyk_{y\to y^{\prime}}x^{y} as a flow from the vertex yy to the vertex y′y^{\prime}, then condition (3) says that at each vertex of the graph GG, the sum of all the incoming flows equals the sum of all outgoing flows. The identity (3) implies that the graph GG is weakly reversible [16].

The name “toric dynamical system” has been introduced [10] in order to emphasize the remarkable algebraic properties of these systems, but this class of polynomial dynamical systems has been first studied in depth in the 1972 breakthrough paper of Horn and Jackson [16], where they have been called complex balanced mass-action systems. Also in [16] Horn and Jackson have shown that these systems enjoy remarkable stability properties, and in particular they have a unique positive equilibrium within each linear invariant subspace, and this equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable. Actually, in [16] Horn and Jackson stated that the unique positive equilibrium within each linear invariant subspace is a global attractor99 9 i.e., if the positive equilibrium x0x_{0} belongs to the linear invariant subspace 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0}, then all trajectories that start in 𝒮0\mathcal{S}_{0} converge to x0x_{0}. , but soon afterwards Horn explained that they have not actually proved this claim, and in 1974 he proposed this global convergence property as a conjecture [17].

The conjecture that toric dynamical systems have a global attractor within each linear invariant subspace (or, in the language of Horn, that complex balanced mass-action systems have a global attractor within each reaction simplex) was later called the global attractor conjecture [10].

The global attractor conjecture has resisted efforts for a proof for over five decades, but proofs of many special cases have been obtained during this time, for example [21, 22, 10, 4, 5, 19, 3, 18].

In particular, Craciun, Nazarov and Pantea [3] have proved the three-dimensional case, and Pantea has generalized this result for the case where the dimension of the linear invariant subspaces is at most three [18]. Using a different approach, Anderson has proved the conjecture under the additional hypothesis that the graph GG has a single connected component [5], and this result has been generalized by Gopalkrishnan, Miller, and Shiu for the case where the graph GG is strongly endotactic [15].

The results described above do not provide a proof of the global attractor conjecture in full generality, and also do not provide a proof for any of the following three important special cases: (i)(i) the case where GG is reversible1010 10 i.e., if y→y′∈Gy\to y^{\prime}\in G then also y′→y∈Gy^{\prime}\to y\in G. , (i​i)(ii) the case where GG is reversible and the system (1) is detailed balanced1111 11 i.e., we replace the vertex-balance equilibrium condition (3) with the more restrictive edge-balance equilibrium condition: ky→y¯​x0y=ky¯→y​x0y¯k_{y\to\overline{y}}x_{0}^{y}=k_{\overline{y}\to y}x_{0}^{\overline{y}} for all y→y¯∈Gy\to\overline{y}\in G. This condition says that, at the equilibrium point x0x_{0}, the “forward flux” balances the “reverse flux” for any edge in GG. , and (i​i​i)(iii) the case where GG is reversible and ky→y′=ky′→yk_{y\to y^{\prime}}=k_{y^{\prime}\to y} for all y→y′∈Gy\to y^{\prime}\in G.

The goal of this paper is to use toric differential inclusions in order to construct a proof of the global attractor conjecture in full generality.

Toric differential inclusions are defined as follows1212 12 See section 4.1 for more details and examples.. Consider a finite set ℱ\mathcal{F} of polyhedral cones1313 13 A polyhedral cone in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is the intersection of a finite set of half-spaces of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. that cover ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, such that ℱ\mathcal{F} is a polyhedral fan1414 14 A polyhedral fan in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is a finite set ℱ\mathcal{F} of polyhedral cones such that (i)(i) any face of a cone in ℱ\mathcal{F} is also in ℱ\mathcal{F}, and (i​i)(ii) the intersection of two cones in ℱ\mathcal{F} is a face of both cones. Simple examples of polyhedral fans ℱℋ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{H}} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} are given by the polyhedral cones delimited by a finite set ℋ\mathcal{H} of hyperplanes that contain the origin. This particular case of “hyperplane-generated polyhedral fan” is especially relevant for motivating our definition of toric differential inclusions.  [29, 30], and fix some real number δ>0\delta>0. For each cone C∈ℱC\in\mathcal{F} denote by CoC^{o} the polar cone1515 15 The polar cone of a cone C∈ℝnC\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the cone Co={y∈ℝn|x⋅y≤0​ for all ​x∈C}C^{o}=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}|\ x\cdot y\leq 0\textrm{ for all }x\in C\} [31]. of CC. Then for each x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} define Fℱ,δ​(x)F_{\mathcal{F},\delta}(x) to be the convex cone generated by the union of polar cones CoC^{o} for all C∈ℱC\in\mathcal{F} such that d​i​s​t​(x,C)<δdist(x,C)<\delta. Then a toric differential inclusion is a differential inclusion on ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0} given by

d​xd​t∈Fℱ,δ​(log⁡x).\frac{dx}{dt}\in F_{\mathcal{F},\delta}(\log x). (4)

It turns out that, although the global attractor conjecture is formulated in terms of some systems if the form (1), it will be very useful to understand some properties of systems of the form (4) in order to construct a proof of the conjecture. Indeed, we can “embed” some systems of the form (1) (and even some systems of the form (2)) into toric differential inclusions:

Theorem A. If a polynomial dynamical system has a representation (2) such that GG is weakly reversible and the non-negative functions ky→y′​(t)k_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t) are bounded away from zero and infinity, then it can be embedded1616 16 We say that the dynamical system d​xd​t=f⁡(x)\frac{dx}{dt}=f(x) is embedded into the differential inclusion d​xd​t∈F⁡(x)\frac{dx}{dt}\in F(x) in the domain Ω\Omega, if f⁡(x)∈F⁡(x)f(x)\in F(x) for all x∈Ωx\in\Omega. in a toric differential inclusion.

The theorem has already been proved in [2]. In particular, it follows that if GG is weakly reversible, then (1) can be embedded in a toric differential inclusion for any choice of parameters ky→y′>0k_{y\to y^{\prime}}\!>\!0. We then prove that, for any toric differential inclusion 𝒯\mathcal{T} and for any positive point x0∈ℝ>0nx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}, there exists a hypersurface ℋ⊂ℝ>0n\mathcal{H}\subset\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} that separates ℝ≥0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\geq 0} into two regions, such that ∂ℝ>0n\partial\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} and x0x_{0} are in different regions, and the “upper” region of ℋ\mathcal{H} (i.e., the region that contains the point x0x_{0}) is at positive distance from ∂ℝ>0n\partial\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}, and is a forward-invariant region for the solutions of 𝒯\mathcal{T} that remain inside some cube [0,M]n[0,M]^{n}. We will refer to this kind of hypersurface ℋ\mathcal{H} as a zero-separating hypersurface1717 17 Note that the (fundamental) notion of “zero-separating hypersurface” here is different from (but still very similar with) the identically-named notion of “zero-separating hypersurface” in [1]. See section 4 for more details.:

Theorem B. Toric differential inclusions have an exhaustive1818 18 For our goals, it is not sufficient to construct a single zero-separating hypersurface; instead we need a family of zero-separating hypersurfaces 𝒵ε\mathcal{Z}_{\varepsilon} such that for any x0∈ℝ>0nx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} there exists some ε\varepsilon such that x0x_{0} is in the “upper” region of 𝒵ε\mathcal{Z}_{\varepsilon}. This is called an exhaustive family of zero-separating hypersurfaces. family of zero-separating hypersurfaces.

Most of our effort in this paper will be spent on the proof of Theorem B. Then we will use this result to conclude that trajectories of toric dynamical systems must stay away from the boundary of ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}:

Theorem C. Toric dynamical systems are persistent.

Finally, we will be able to conclude that the global attractor conjecture is true:

Theorem D. Toric dynamical systems have a globally attracting point within each positive linear invariant subspace.

2 Definitions and notation

As we mentioned in the previous section, some of the main objects of interest in this paper are non-autonomous polynomial dynamical systems of the form (2) such that the graph GG is weakly reversible, and the nonnegative scalar functions ky→y′​(t)k_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t) are bounded away from zero and infinity. We will refer to this class of dynamical systems as variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical systems1919 19 Variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical systems have also been called variable-kk toric dynamical systems [1], because any such dynamical system can be obtained from a toric dynamical system by using the same graph GG, and replacing the constants ky→y′k_{y\to y^{\prime}} with time-dependent non-negative functions ky→y′​(t)k_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t) that are bounded away from zero and infinity. .

More precisely, a variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical system is a dynamical system on ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0} of the form

d​xd​t=∑y→y′∈Gky→y′​(t)​xy​(y′−y)\frac{dx}{dt}=\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}\in G}k_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t)\,x^{y}(y^{\prime}-y) (5)

such that GG is weakly reversible, and there exists a fixed positive number ε\varepsilon such that ε≤ky→y′​(t)≤1ε\varepsilon\leq k_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t)\leq\frac{1}{\varepsilon} for all tt and for all y→y′∈Gy\to y^{\prime}\in G.

Note that, under these conditions, solutions of the variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical system above are also solutions of the differential inclusion on ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0} given by

d​xd​t∈F(x),whereF(x)={∑y→y′∈Gky→y′xy(y′−y)|ε≤ky→y′≤1ε}.\frac{dx}{dt}\in F(x),\mathrm{\ where\ }F(x)=\left\{\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}\in G}k_{y\to y^{\prime}}\,x^{y}(y^{\prime}-y)\ \ |\ \ \varepsilon\leq k_{y\to y^{\prime}}\leq\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right\}. (6)

We will show that solutions of the differential inclusion (6) are also solutions of a type of differential inclusions with rich geometric properties, called toric differential inclusions. Later in this section we will define the general notion of toric differential inclusions in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0}. We first define the class of polar differential inclusions in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

2.1 Polar differential inclusions

If the graph GG is reversible, then the equations (5) can be written as

d​xd​t=∑y⇌y′∈G(ky→y′​(t)​xy−ky′→y​(t)​xy′)​(y′−y),\frac{dx}{dt}=\sum_{y\rightleftharpoons y^{\prime}\in G}\left(k_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t)x^{y}-k_{y^{\prime}\to y}(t)x^{y^{\prime}}\right)(y^{\prime}-y), (7)

by grouping together terms given by an edge y→y′y\to y^{\prime} and its reverse y′→yy^{\prime}\to y. Then, for each reversible edge y⇌y′∈Gy\rightleftharpoons y^{\prime}\in G, there is now a single term in the sum (7), which can be thought of as a “tug-of-war” between the forward and reverse terms. Indeed, both the forward and the reverse terms are trying to “push” the state x⁡(t)x(t) of the system along the same line2020 20 i.e., a line whose direction is given by the vector y′−yy^{\prime}-y. , but in opposite directions. Then, the domain ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0} can be partitioned into three regions: the region where the inequality ε​xy≥1ε​xy′\varepsilon x^{y}\geq\frac{1}{\varepsilon}x^{y^{\prime}} holds (which implies ky→y′​(t)​xy≥ky′→y​(t)​xy′k_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t)x^{y}\geq k_{y^{\prime}\to y}(t)x^{y^{\prime}}), the region where the inequality 1ε​xy≤ε​xy′\frac{1}{\varepsilon}x^{y}\leq\varepsilon x^{y^{\prime}} holds (which implies ky→y′​(t)​xy≤ky′→y​(t)​xy′k_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t)x^{y}\leq k_{y^{\prime}\to y}(t)x^{y^{\prime}}), and an uncertainty region where neither one of these two inequalities are satisfied, and either one of the two terms ky→y′​(t)​xyk_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t)x^{y} and ky′→y​(t)​xy′k_{y^{\prime}\to y}(t)x^{y^{\prime}} may win the tug-of-war, due to the fact that ky→y′​(t)k_{y\to y^{\prime}}(t) and ky′→y​(t)k_{y^{\prime}\to y}(t) may take any values between ε\varepsilon and 1ε\frac{1}{\varepsilon}. Some concrete examples can be found in Section 3 of [3]. In particular, note that if one term does win the tug-of-war, then the direction of the sum of the two terms is towards the uncertainty region, and also towards the hypersurface xy=xy′x^{y}=x^{y^{\prime}} in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0}.

The simplest way to understand how these regions adjoin each other is to look at them in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} instead of ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0}, after applying a logarithmic transformation. If we denote X=log⁡xX=\log x, then the hypersurface xy=xy′x^{y}=x^{y^{\prime}} becomes the hyperplane (y′−y)⋅X=0(y^{\prime}-y)\cdot X=0. Moreover, the uncertainty region described above becomes just the set of points at distance <δ=2​|log⁡ε|‖y′−y‖<\delta=\frac{2|\!\log\varepsilon|}{||y^{\prime}-y||} from this hyperplane. Note also that the direction given by the vector y′−yy^{\prime}-y is exactly the direction orthogonal to the hyperplane (y′−y)⋅X=0(y^{\prime}-y)\cdot X=0.

Therefore, if the graph GG consists of a single reversible edge y⇌y′y\rightleftharpoons y^{\prime}, then the dynamics of the system (7) at a point xx can be described as follows: we know that xx will move along a line of support vector (y′−y)(y^{\prime}-y), and we are able to specify one direction or another by mapping xx to X=log⁡xX=\log x, and checking whether the distance between XX and the hyperplane (y′−y)⋅X=0(y^{\prime}-y)\cdot X=0 is ≥δ\geq\delta. Moreover, if we can specify this direction, then it is always the direction towards (and not away from) this hyperplane, and orthogonal to it.

This characterization has the advantage that it can be carried over to the more general case, where GG contains several reversible edges. In that case we have several tug-of-wars going on at the same time, but for each one of them we can specify the winning direction (if any) at xx by calculating the distance between X=log⁡xX=\log x and some hyperplane in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Depending on whether XX falls outside an uncertainty region or not, each reversible edge y⇌y′y\rightleftharpoons y^{\prime} of GG contributes one or two resultant vectors (if one, then it is either y′−yy^{\prime}-y or y−y′y-y^{\prime}, and if two, then they are ±(y′−y)\pm(y^{\prime}-y)).

If follows that any system (7) can be embedded into a differential inclusion on ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0} given by a set ℋ\mathcal{H} of hyperplanes in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and a number δ>0\delta>0, as follows. For each x∈ℝ>0nx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0} we define Fℋ,δ​(log⁡x)F_{\mathcal{H},\delta}(\log x) to be the convex cone generated by vectors orthogonal to the hyperplanes of ℋ\mathcal{H}, in the direction that goes from the point X=log⁡xX=\log x towards each hyperplane, and also the opposite direction if XX is at distance <δ<\delta from some hyperplane. If XX does not belong to any uncertainty region, then Fℋ,δ​(log⁡x)F_{\mathcal{H},\delta}(\log x) is defined to be exactly the polar cone CoC^{o} of a cone CC bounded by a subset of hyperplanes2121 21 the cone CC is the largest cone that contains the point XX within the polyhedral fan ℱ⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{H}) determined by the set of hyperplanes ℋ\mathcal{H}. The convex cone generated by the “outer normal” vectors orthogonal to the hyperplane faces of CC is its polar cone CoC^{o} [30]. from ℋ\mathcal{H}. Moreover, if XX does belong to some uncertainty regions, then we can still describe Fℋ,δ​(log⁡x)F_{\mathcal{H},\delta}(\log x) in terms of polar cones, by including not just the polar of the largest cone of ℱ⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{H}) that contains XX, but also the polar of each cone of ℱ⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{H}) that is at distance ≤δ\leq\delta from XX.

Of course, not all polyhedral fans are determined by a set of hyperplanes as above. Nevertheless, we can generalize the construction described above to define polar differential inclusions given by a polyhedral fan ℱ\mathcal{F} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, as described in the previous section: we define Fℱ,δ​(X)F_{\mathcal{F},\delta}(X) to be the convex cone generated by the union of polar cones CoC^{o} for all C∈ℱC\in\mathcal{F} such that d​i​s​t​(X,C)<δdist(X,C)<\delta.

2.2 Toric differential inclusions

Polar differential inclusions can produce sets of cones that contain the right-hand-side of the vector fields (5) for reversible GG, but they are defined on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, while the system (5) is defined on ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0}. To obtain a proper embedding we need to introduce toric differential inclusions, which are obtained from polar differential inclusions by a logarithmic transformation: a toric differential inclusion given by a polyhedral fan ℱ\mathcal{F} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is a differential inclusion on ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0} given by

d​xd​t∈Fℱ,δ​(log⁡x)\frac{dx}{dt}\in F_{\mathcal{F},\delta}(\log x) (8)

where Fℱ,δF_{\mathcal{F},\delta} is a polar differential inclusion as defined above.

Due to the way this definition is related to the system (7), it follows that variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical systems (5) that are generated by a reversible graph GG can be embedded into polar differential inclusions.

As we discussed above, for a reversible graph GG, the polyhedral fan ℱ\mathcal{F} could be chosen simply as the fan generated by the set of hyperplanes that are orthogonal to the vectors y′−yy^{\prime}-y for y→y′∈Gy\to y^{\prime}\in G.

We need to remove this strong assumption of reversibility, in order to be able to address the global attractor conjecture in full generality. In the next section we explain how to find such a polyhedral fan for any weakly reversible graph GG.

3 Embedding of variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical systems into toric differential inclusions

As we discussed in the previous section, the simplest examples of polar differential inclusions are generated by polyhedral fans ℱℋ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{H}} that are determined by a finite set ℋ\mathcal{H} of hyperplanes2222 22 i.e., ℱℋ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{H}} consists of all the cones delimited by hyperplanes in ℋ\mathcal{H}. that pass through the origin. Then, the simplest examples of toric differential inclusions are also generated by polyhedral fans ℱℋ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{H}} as above. We will refer to this class of toric differential inclusions as hyperplane-generated toric differential inclusions.

We have seen in the previous section that any reversible variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical system in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0} can be embedded into a (hyperplane-generated) toric differential inclusion. Here we show that a similar fact is true for all variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical systems2323 23 In order to prove the global attractor conjecture we plan to construct some forward-invariant sets for any given toric dynamical system (not just for the reversible ones). Theorem 3.1 will help us argue that we can accomplish our goal by constructing something called zero-separating surfaces (ZSH) for toric differential inclusions. .

Theorem 3.1.

Consider a variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical system (5). Then this system can be embedded into a toric differential inclusion.

Proof.

This theorem has already been proved in [2]. We discuss a sketch of the proof below, see [2] for more details.

Assume first that the weakly reversible graph GG is made up of a single directed cycle. If our single-cycle graph is given by y1→y2→…→yr→y1y_{1}\to y_{2}\to...\to y_{r}\to y_{1}, then the variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical system it generates is of the form

d​xd​t=∑i=1rki​(t)​xyi​(yi+1−yi),\frac{dx}{dt}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}k_{i}(t)\,x^{y_{i}}(y_{i+1}-y_{i}), (9)

where yr+1=y1y_{r+1}=y_{1} and ε0≤ki​(t)≤1ε0\varepsilon_{0}\leq k_{i}(t)\leq\frac{1}{\varepsilon_{0}} for some ε0>0{\varepsilon_{0}}>0.

Consider the set ℒ\mathcal{L} of lines through the origin in the direction of vectors yi−yjy_{i}-y_{j} for all i≠ji\neq j, and denote by ℋ\mathcal{H} the set of all hyperplanes that are orthogonal complements of lines in ℒ\mathcal{L}2424 24 i.e., a hyperplane belongs to ℋ\mathcal{H} iff it is orthogonal to a line in ℒ\mathcal{L}. . Denote by ℱℋ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{H}} the polyhedral fan generated by the set of hyperplanes ℋ\mathcal{H}, and, for δ>0\delta>0, denote by 𝒯ℋ,δ\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{H},\delta} the corresponding hyperplane-generated toric differential inclusion. We will show that there exists δ0>0\delta_{0}>0 such that the single-cycle variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical system (9) is embedded in the toric differential inclusion 𝒯ℋ,δ0\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{H},\delta_{0}}.

Choose δ0>0\delta_{0}>0 large enough such that the uncertainty regions given by the reversible edges yi⇌yjy_{i}\rightleftharpoons y_{j} and ε0\varepsilon_{0} are contained within the uncertainty regions of the toric differential inclusion 𝒯ℋ,δ0\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{H},\delta_{0}}.

Fix a point x∈ℝ>0nx\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} such that X=log⁡xX=\log x belongs to some cone CC in ℱℋ\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{H}}, and does not belong to any uncertainty region of 𝒯ℋ,δ0\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{H},\delta_{0}}. In particular, it follows that the cone CC has dimension nn, otherwise XX would be contained in some hyperplane in ℋ\mathcal{H}, which in turn would be contained in an uncertainty region of 𝒯ℋ,δ0\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{H},\delta_{0}}. We want to show that the right-hand-side of (9) is contained in the dual cone CoC^{o}.

Consider a vector ww in the interior of CC, and project y1,y2,…,yry_{1},y_{2},...,y_{r} on the line lwl_{w} that passes through the origin in the direction given by ww. Then no two projections are the same, because ww does not belong to any of the hyperplanes in ℋ\mathcal{H}. We now give a second set of names to the vectors y1,y2,…,yry_{1},y_{2},...,y_{r}, say v1,v2,…,vrv_{1},v_{2},...,v_{r}, to record the distance to the origin of the projections along the line (i.e., if the projection of yi1y_{i_{1}} is the closest to origin, then v1=yi1v_{1}=y_{i_{1}}, and if the projection of yi2y_{i_{2}} is the second closest to origin, then v2=yi2v_{2}=y_{i_{2}}, and so on). Note that, since the interior of CC is disjoint from all the hyperplanes in ℋ\mathcal{H}, it follows that the new names v1,v2,…,vrv_{1},v_{2},...,v_{r} do not depend on the particular choice of vector ww in the interior of CC. In other words, the dot products (vl+1−vl)⋅w(v_{l+1}-v_{l})\cdot w are all negative numbers, for all ww in the interior of CC. Therefore, the vectors v2−v1,v3−v2,…,vr−vr−1v_{2}-v_{1},v_{3}-v_{2},...,v_{r}-v_{r-1} belong to CoC^{o}.

So, in order to show that the right-hand side of (9) is included in CoC^{o}, it is enough to show that it can be written as a positive linear combination of the vectors v2−v1,v3−v2,…,vr−vr−1v_{2}-v_{1},v_{3}-v_{2},...,v_{r}-v_{r-1}.

Note that (i1,i2,…,ir)(i_{1},i_{2},...,i_{r}) is a permutation of (1,2,…,r)(1,2,...,r). If we denote the inverse permutation by (j1,j2,…,jr)(j_{1},j_{2},...,j_{r}), it follows that y1=vj1y_{1}=v_{j_{1}}, y2=vj2y_{2}=v_{j_{2}}, and so on.

Then we have y2−y1=vj2−vj1y_{2}-y_{1}=v_{j_{2}}-v_{j_{1}}. If j2>j1j_{2}>j_{1} we write

y2−y1=∑l=j1j2−1(vl+1−vl),y_{2}-y_{1}=\sum_{l=j_{1}}^{j_{2}-1}(v_{l+1}-v_{l}),

and if j2<j1j_{2}<j_{1} we write

y2−y1=−∑l=j2j1−1(vl+1−vl),y_{2}-y_{1}=-\sum_{l=j_{2}}^{j_{1}-1}(v_{l+1}-v_{l}),

We do the same for y3−y2,y4−y3y_{3}-y_{2},\ y_{4}-y_{3}, and so on. This way, we write each difference yi+1−yiy_{i+1}-y_{i} from the right-hand-side of (9) in terms of the vectors ±(yl+1−yl)\pm(y_{l+1}-y_{l}), with l=1,2,…,r−1l=1,2,...,r-1. Therefore we can re-group terms to obtain

d​xd​t=∑i=1r−1Φl​(vl+1−vl),\frac{dx}{dt}=\sum_{i=1}^{r-1}\Phi_{l}(v_{l+1}-v_{l}), (10)

where Φl\Phi_{l} is a sum of several terms of the form ki​xvik_{i}\,x^{v_{i}}, with various signs.

Note now that the positive terms inside Φl\Phi_{l} correspond to edges of the form vm→vnv_{m}\to v_{n} with m≤l<nm\leq l<n, and negative terms inside Φl\Phi_{l} correspond to edges of the form vm→vnv_{m}\to v_{n} with n≤l<mn\leq l<m. This means that the positive terms inside Φl\Phi_{l} contain ki​xvik_{i}\,x^{v_{i}} with i≤li\leq l, and the negative terms inside Φl\Phi_{l} contain ki​xvik_{i}\,x^{v_{i}} with i>li>l. Since log⁡x∈C\log x\in C (and is not in an uncertainty region), and due to our choice of δ0\delta_{0}, it follows that k1​xv1<k2​xv2<…<kr​xvrk_{1}x^{v_{1}}<k_{2}x^{v_{2}}<...<k_{r}x^{v_{r}}. Therefore, the sum of the positive terms inside Φl\Phi_{l} dominates the sum of the negative terms inside Φl\Phi_{l}, for each ll2525 25 note that the number of positive terms inside Φl\Phi_{l} is the same as the number of negative terms inside Φl\Phi_{l}, because the graph GG is a cycle. . In conclusion, the right-hand-side of (10) (and therefore (9)) is a positive linear combination of the vectors vl+1−vlv_{l+1}-v_{l}, for 1≤l≤r−11\leq l\leq r-1, so it belongs to CoC^{o}.

If xx does belong to an uncertainty region of the toric differential inclusion 𝒯ℋ,δ0\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{H},\delta_{0}}, then denote by F⁡(x)F(x) the cone of 𝒯ℋ,δ0\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{H},\delta_{0}} at xx. It follows that the maximal linear subspace contained in F⁡(x)F(x) has dimension ≥1\geq 1 in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. We project the problem on the orthogonal complement of that subspace, and then we reason the same way as above2626 26 When projecting on the smaller dimensional subspace, the graph GG is replaced by its projection G~\tilde{G}. All vertices of GG that project to the same vertex of G~\tilde{G} are interchangeable with each other when checking that the right-hand-side of (9) is contained in the (degenerate) cone F⁡(x)F(x), because the projections are done along linear subspaces contained in F⁡(x)F(x). . This gives us the desired conclusion for the case when GG is made up of a single directed cycle.

If the weakly reversible graph GG is not a single directed cycle, then we write it as a union of cyclic graphs, G=⋃i=1gGi\displaystyle G=\bigcup_{i=1}^{g}G_{i}, and we can argue as above for each such GiG_{i}. We obtain that the variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical systems given by the cycle GiG_{i} are embedded in toric differential inclusions generated by some set of hyperplanes ℋi\mathcal{H}_{i}. Note now that the right-hand-side of a variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical system given by GG can be decomposed into a sum of terms, such that each term is of the form2727 27 We may have to use smaller εi\varepsilon_{i} values for the terms in the decomposition, because the same edge of GG may belong to several (but of course only finitely many) graphs GiG_{i}. given by the right-hand-side of a variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical system determined by GiG_{i}. Then we conclude that any variable-kk mass-action system given by GG can be embedded into a toric differential inclusion generated by the set of hyperplanes ℋ=⋃i=1gℋi\displaystyle\mathcal{H}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{g}\mathcal{H}_{i}. ∎

4 Strategy for the proof of the global attractor conjecture: the big picture

In order to prove the global attractor conjecture we will prove that toric dynamical systems are persistent. It has been known for a long time that persistence of toric dynamical systems, together with a simple application of the LaSalle invariance principle would immediately imply global stability [21, 22, 32].

More precisely, we will prove the following stronger fact: for any positive initial condition x0∈ℝ>0nx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} of a toric dynamical system there exists a compact forward invariant region Kx0⊂ℝ>0nK_{x_{0}}\subset\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} such that x0∈Kx0x_{0}\in K_{x_{0}}. Of course, this implies that toric dynamical systems are persistent.

In order to accomplish this goal, our main focus will be the construction of a specific type of hypersurfaces in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} called zero-separating hypersurfaces (ZSH), which, when considered together with well-chosen level sets of the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function, give rise to compact forward invariant regions Kx0K_{x_{0}} like we mentioned above; see Figure 2 for a two-dimensional example (in this example the ZSH is just a curve).

More precisely, our strategy will be to construct polyhedral zero-separating hypersurfaces (polyhedral ZSH). Our construction of a polyhedral ZSH will rely on a ZSH blueprint. A ZSH blueprint is a structure associated to a given polyhedral fan, which contains inside complete instructions for the construction of an exhaustive family of ZSH. Polyhedral fans are relevant because of the theorem on embedding toric dynamical systems into toric differential inclusions; and a toric differential inclusion (denoted 𝒯ℱ,δ\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{F},\delta}) is given by a polyhedral fan ℱ\mathcal{F} and a positive number δ\delta.

In our construction of polyhedral ZSH we will see that the specific number δ\delta above will practically become irrelevant, and it will turn out that we will not need to look in much depth at detailed properties of toric differential inclusions; it will be sufficient to focus almost exclusively on the much simpler notion of polyhedral fan.

Therefore, given a polyhedral fan ℱ\mathcal{F}, we will develop a step-by-step process that allows us to construct some polyhedral hypersurfaces associated to ℱ\mathcal{F}. More precisely, we will show how to construct such families of polyhedral hypersurfaces by taking advantage of a ZSH blueprint, and we will see later that these hypersurfaces are indeed zero-separating hypersurfaces.

In summary, we will proceed according to the following plan2828 28 For convenience of notation we assume that we start in (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional space; then the fundamentals steps (i.e., Steps 2 and 3) take place in nn-dimensional space.:

Step 0. Given a toric dynamical system 𝐓n+1\mathbf{T}_{n+1} in ℝ>0n+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_{>0}, we embed it into a toric differential inclusion 𝒯n+1\mathcal{T}_{n+1}, generated by a polyhedral fan ℱn+1\mathcal{F}_{n+1} and a number δ>0\delta>0.

Step 1. Given the polyhedral fan ℱn+1\mathcal{F}_{n+1} in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1} we construct the x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivision 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} generated by ℱn+1\mathcal{F}_{n+1}.

Step 2. Given the x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivision 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} we construct a ZSH blueprint ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} for 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n}.

Step 3. Given the ZSH blueprint ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} we construct an exhaustive family of nn-dimensional polyhedral ZSHs denoted 𝒵ε\mathcal{Z}_{\varepsilon} in ℝ>0n+1\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n+1}.

Step 4. We show that for any x0∈ℝ>0n+1x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n+1} there exists a polyhedral hypersurface 𝒵ε\mathcal{Z}_{\varepsilon} among the ones that we have constructed in step 3, such that 𝒵ε\mathcal{Z}_{\varepsilon} (together with a well-chosen level set of the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function) determines a compact set Kx0⊂ℝ>0n+1K_{x_{0}}\subset\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n+1} such that x0∈Kx0x_{0}\in K_{x_{0}} and Kx0K_{x_{0}} is a forward invariant region for the toric dynamical system 𝐓n+1\mathbf{T}_{n+1} that we started with in Step 0.

Step 0 has already been done in [2], and we have discussed it in section 3. Step 1 will not be difficult, but we will need to we restrict our attention (without loss of generality) to x1x_{1}-xn+1x_{n+1}-fans. Steps 2 and 3 are very much interconnected, and most of our effort will focus on these two steps. Step 4 will be a relatively quick corollary of the previous steps.

4.1 Polyhedral fans and toric differential inclusions

In this subsection we revisit some definitions and results that have also been mentioned in a previous section, and we look at a few simple examples that illustrate these notions. The reader who is familiar with the notions and results from the previous sections can skip this subsection.

Definition 4.1.

A polyhedral fan in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is a finite collection ℱ\mathcal{F} of closed convex polyhedral cones2929 29 All the cones we are interested in here are closed convex polyhedral cones; therefore, from now on, whenever we say “cone”, we mean “closed convex polyhedral cone”. in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n},

ℱ={C1,…,Cm},\mathcal{F}=\{C_{1},...,C_{m}\},

such that we have

(i)(i) for any cone Ci∈ℱC_{i}\in\mathcal{F} any face of CiC_{i} also belongs to ℱ\mathcal{F},

and

(i​i)(ii) for any Ci,Cj∈ℱC_{i},C_{j}\in\mathcal{F} their intersection Ci∩CjC_{i}\cap C_{j} is a common face of both of them.

We say that the polyhedral fan ℱ\mathcal{F} is pointed if any cone C∈ℱC\in\mathcal{F} is a pointed cone. Also, we say that a polyhedral fan ℱ\mathcal{F} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is complete if the union of all the cones in ℱ\mathcal{F} is the whole ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Here we are only interested in pointed and complete polyhedral fans, and for simplicity we will refer to them simply as fans (in other words, from now on whenever we say ‘‘fan”, we mean ‘‘pointed and complete polyhedral fan”)3030 30 In some instances we will need to refer to the set of all the cones of a fan ℱ\mathcal{F} that are contained in a specific subset of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}; in this case we will say “restricted fan”..

See Figure 3(a)(a) for an illustration of a fan in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. This fan consists of 13 cones: six cones of dimension 2, six cones of dimension 1, and one cone of dimension 0 (i.e., the origin of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}).

Definition 4.2.

Given a fan ℱ\mathcal{F} and a real number δ>0\delta>0 we define the
toric differential inclusion generated by ℱ\mathcal{F} and δ\delta as follows. For any x∈ℝ>0nx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0} we consider all the cones Cj∈ℱC_{j}\in\mathcal{F} such that dist​(log⁡x,Cj)<δ\text{dist}(\log x,C_{j})<\delta and define Fℱ,δ​(x){F}_{\mathcal{F},\delta}(x) to be the cone generated by the union of all polar cones Cj∘C_{j}^{\circ} . Then the toric differential inclusion generated by ℱ\mathcal{F} and δ\delta is given by

d​xd​t∈Fℱ,δ​(x).\frac{dx}{dt}\in{F}_{\mathcal{F},\delta}(x). (11)

For example, in the case of the fan ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} shown in Figure 3(a)(a), we can see that the right-hand side of the corresponding toric differential inclusion (i.e., Fℱ2,δ​(x){F}_{\mathcal{F}_{2},\delta}(x)) consists of a piecewise constant choice of convex cones (one for each Cj∈ℱ2C_{j}\in\mathcal{F}_{2}), as shown in Figure 3(c)(c).

Toric differential inclusions are useful in the study of the global attractor conjecture because of the following embedding theorem [2], which implies that one can reduce the problem of building forward-invariant regions for toric dynamical systems to the analogous problem for toric differential inclusions.

Theorem 4.3.

Consider a variable-kk weakly reversible3131 31 Note that toric dynamical systems are special cases of weakly reversible systems; in particular, every toric dynamical system has a fixed vector of parameters (i.e., reaction rate constants) kk, but not every weakly reversible system with a fixed vector of parameters is a toric dynamical system (because, in general, the “vertex balance condition” is sufficient but not necessary for weak reversibility). dynamical system. Then this dynamical system can be embedded into a toric differential inclusion. More precisely, if our variable-kk weakly reversible dynamical system is given by

d​xd​t=f⁡(t,x),\frac{dx}{dt}=f(t,x),

then there exists a fan ℱ\mathcal{F} and some δ>0\delta>0 such that we have

f⁡(t,x)∈Fℱ,δ​(x),f(t,x)\in{F}_{\mathcal{F},\delta}(x),

for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} and all x∈ℝ>0nx\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}.

4.2 Forward invariant regions and ZSH for toric differential inclusions

We are interested in constructing forward-invariant regions for toric differential inclusions. Let us first define the following notion:

Definition 4.4.

Consider a piecewise smooth surface 𝒵\mathcal{Z} in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}, and a toric differential inclusion 𝒯\mathcal{T} in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} generated by a fan ℱ\mathcal{F} and a number δ>0\delta>0. If PP is a smooth point of 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, we say that 𝒯\mathcal{T} cannot cross 𝒵\mathcal{Z} at PP if the tangent hyperplane of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} at PP is a supporting hyperplane of the cone Fℱ,δ​(P)F_{\mathcal{F},\delta}(P). Also, for a set Ω∈ℝ>0n\Omega\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}, we say that 𝒯\mathcal{T} cannot cross 𝒵\mathcal{Z} within Ω\Omega if 𝒯\mathcal{T} cannot cross 𝒵\mathcal{Z} at any smooth point P∈ΩP\in\Omega.

Let us note the following simple characterization of the condition that 𝒯\mathcal{T} cannot cross 𝒵\mathcal{Z} at PP:

Remark 4.5.

Consider a piecewise smooth surface 𝒵\mathcal{Z} in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}, and a toric differential inclusion 𝒯\mathcal{T} in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} generated by a fan ℱ\mathcal{F} and a number δ>0\delta>0. Consider a smooth point of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} denoted PP. Then 𝒯\mathcal{T} cannot cross 𝒵\mathcal{Z} at PP if and only if there exists a normal vector n→P\vec{n}_{P} of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} at PP such that n→P∈𝒞\vec{n}_{P}\in\mathcal{C} for any cone 𝒞∈ℱ\mathcal{C}\in\mathcal{F} that satisfies the condition

dist⁡(𝒞,log⁡P)<δ.\mathrm{dist}(\mathcal{C},\log P)<\delta.

Indeed, this follows immediately from the definition of the cone Fℱ,δ​(P)F_{\mathcal{F},\delta}(P) in (11), together with the general observation that the cone generated by a union of polar cones equals the polar cone of the intersection of those cones [31].

The key notion in this section is the zero-separating hypersurface, or ZSH for short:

Definition 4.6.

Consider a piecewise smooth surface 𝒵\mathcal{Z} in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}, and a toric differential inclusion 𝒯\mathcal{T} in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} generated by a fan ℱ\mathcal{F} and a number δ>0\delta>0. We say that 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is a zero-separating hypersurface for 𝒯\mathcal{T} (or 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is ZSH for 𝒯\mathcal{T}) if the following are true:

(i)(i) there exists some η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1) such that

𝒵⊂ℝ>0n∖(η+ℝ>0n),\mathcal{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}\setminus(\eta+\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}),

(i​i)(ii) 𝒵\mathcal{Z} intersects every toric ray3232 32 A toric ray in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is the image via the exponential function of a line that passes through the origin of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Note that every toric ray is contained in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} and passes through the point of coordinates (1,1,…,1)∈ℝ>0n(1,1,\dots,1)\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}. in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} exactly once,

and

(i​i​i)(iii) there exists some M≥1M\geq 1 such that the toric differential inclusion 𝒯\mathcal{T} cannot cross 𝒵\mathcal{Z} within the set (0,M)n(0,M)^{n}.

Recall that, given a toric differential inclusion 𝒯\mathcal{T} in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}, we want to construct a family of ZSH for 𝒯\mathcal{T} denoted 𝒵ε\mathcal{Z}_{\varepsilon} such that each such ZSH (together with a well-chosen level set of the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function) gives rise to a compact forward invariant set Kε⊂ℝ>0nK_{\varepsilon}\subset\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} for the toric dynamical system that we have started with. Moreover, we want to make sure that for any initial state x0∈ℝ>0nx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} there is some ε\varepsilon such that x0∈Kεx_{0}\in K_{\varepsilon}. Then, as we mentioned before, we obtain a proof of the global attractor conjecture.

Indeed, see Figure 2 for an illustration in ℝ>02\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{2}. More concretely, if we think of the blue polyhedral line in Figure 2 as a ZSH denoted 𝒵ε\mathcal{Z}_{\varepsilon}, we will want the polyhedral line 𝒵ε\mathcal{Z}_{\varepsilon} to get closer and closer to the axes of the positive quadrant as ε\varepsilon gets closer and closer to zero; at the same time, we will want the orange curve (which is a level curve of the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function in ℝ>02\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{2}) to move farther and farther away, so the green forward-invariant region grows bigger and bigger, such that any x0∈ℝ>02x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{2} will be contained to such a green region. In other words, we want the polyhedral lines 𝒵ε\mathcal{Z}_{\varepsilon} to form an exhaustive family of ZSHs.

5 Proof of the global attractor conjecture in the two-dimensional case.

In this section we discuss the proof of the two-dimensional global attractor conjecture, by relying on two-dimensional toric differential inclusions.

Recall that the two-dimensional global attractor conjecture has first been proved in [4], without the use of toric differential inclusions; but, due to the relevance of toric differential inclusions in our proof of the nn-dimensional global attractor conjecture we will focus here on how two-dimensional toric differential inclusions can be used in the proof of the two-dimensional global attractor conjecture. Our main interest is to illustrate the use of toric differential inclusions (and especially polyhedral fans ) in such a proof, where several important aspects of a rich geometric structure of the problem become important, and easy to see.

5.1 Construction of ZSH for two-dimensional toric differential inclusions

Two-dimensional toric differential inclusions admit ZSHs that are polygonal curves, such as the blue curve in Figure 3(d)(d). Note that if this curve is constructed close enough to boundary of the positive quadrant then it does not visit the more complicated regions in the middle of the figure. Therefore, in order to construct such a ZSH it is sufficient for us to focus on the right-hand side of the toric differential inclusion near the boundary of the positive quadrant.

We can see in Figure 3(d)(d) that the (explicitly specified) cones of the toric differential inclusion can be used in order to construct a polygonal curve that cannot be crossed by solutions of toric differential inclusions, and therefore cannot be crossed by solutions of a toric dynamical system that is embedded in this toric differential inclusion (this is discussed in detail in [2]).

More precisely, we can see in Figure 3(e)(e) that the blue polygonal line can be used together with an level set of the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function (the orange curve) to create a forward invariant region that allows us to conclude immediately (using the LaSalle invariance principle [21, 22, 32]) that the global convergence property holds for any solution with initial value inside this region. In other words, the blue polygonal curve is a ZSH.

If we choose some initial point x0∈ℝ>02x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{>0} that is not in this region, then another such forward invariant region can be constructed that contains this x0x_{0}, as follows. First we construct another blue polygonal curve, much closer to the boundary of the positive quadrant. This not only ensures that x0x_{0} lies above this curve, but also ensures that the curve can be extended farther up, and farther to the right3333 33 Note that when we extend the blue curve up or to the right within some uncertainty region for large values of x1x_{1} or x2x_{2}, then it does not satisfy the ZSH property with that uncertainty region. But, if we construct it closer to the boundary of the positive quadrant then we can extended it while preserving the ZSH property farther up and farther to the right.; then we can also intersect it with a level set of the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function that lies above the point x0x_{0}, and obtain another forward invariant region that is now guaranteed to contain x0x_{0}.

Therefore we can conclude the desired global stability result in full generality.

5.2 A different approach: the use of a ZSH blueprint and representations of a fan using subdivisions

In preparation for the higher dimensional cases, we will now discuss a different point of view for the construction of a ZSH in ℝ>02\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{2}, which is similar with the approach shown in Figure 3(d)(d), but emphasizes less the two-dimensional fan; instead, we introduce two (equivalent) notions of subdivisions induced by the fan, which (in this case) are one-dimensional objects that already contain all the relevant information about the two-dimensional fan, see Figures 3(i)(i) and 3(j)(j). Then, to any subdivision we associate a ZSH blueprint (see Figure 3(k)(k)), and we use it as a essential tool that guides our construction of the ZSH. (The ZSH constructed this way will still be a polygonal curve, but we only need to construct it within the set {0<x2≤x1}\{0<x_{2}\leq x_{1}\} because we can then infer the missing half by symmetry, see Figure 3(h)(h).)

Note that, compared to the simplicity of the approach we used in the previous subsection, our approach in this subsection will appear unnecessarily complicated. This is actually true, but, as we mentioned before, our goal in this subsection is not just to construct the ZSH in the two-dimensional case, but to go through each and every step of the more complicated construction that we have to perform in higher dimensions, while we are still in the simplest nontrivial setting: the two-dimensional case.

Consider a fan ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} that is X1X_{1}-X2X_{2}-symmetric, and we also assume3434 34 These assumptions can be made without loss of generality, because, if needed, we are just replacing ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} with a finer version of ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2}; any ZSH for the finer fan will also be a ZSH for the coarser fan, see Lemma 9.3. that the three lines given by {X1=X2}\{X_{1}=X_{2}\}, {X1=0}\{X_{1}=0\}, and {X2=0}\{X_{2}=0\} can be realized as unions of cones that belong to ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2}. Recall that we only need to specify ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} within the (closed) negative orthant; moreover, due to symmetry, we only need to specify ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} within the subset of the negative orthant where we have X2≤X1≤0X_{2}\leq X_{1}\leq 0. Let us denote the restriction of ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} to this subset by ℱ2≤\mathcal{F}_{2}^{\leq} (here the superscript “≤\leq” is meant to remind us the inequality X2≤X1≤0X_{2}\leq X_{1}\leq 0). Then the part of ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} within the negative orthant is uniquely determined by ℱ2≤\mathcal{F}_{2}^{\leq}, and for now on we will focus on ℱ2≤\mathcal{F}_{2}^{\leq}.

Note now that the information within ℱ2≤\mathcal{F}_{2}^{\leq} is completely determined if we specify the subdivision3535 35 By subdivision of 𝒟1H\mathscr{D}_{1}^{H} we mean a finite set of closed intervals and points that cover all of 𝒟1H\mathscr{D}_{1}^{H}, and satisfies properties that are similar to the properties of a fan: any endpoint of an interval of the subdivision is also an element of the subdivision, and the intersection of two intervals of the subdivision is an endpoint of both. ℱ1H\mathcal{F}_{1}^{H} of 𝒟1H\mathscr{D}_{1}^{H}, obtained by considering the sets of the form

(−Ci)∩𝒟1H(-C_{i})\cap\mathscr{D}_{1}^{H}

for all the cones Ci∈ℱ2≤C_{i}\in\mathcal{F}_{2}^{\leq}, where

𝒟1H={(X1H,X2H)∈ℝ≥02|X1H≤X2H​and​X1H+X2H=1},\mathscr{D}_{1}^{H}=\{(X_{1}^{H},X_{2}^{H})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{\geq 0}\ |\ X_{1}^{H}\leq X_{2}^{H}\mathrm{and}\ X_{1}^{H}+X_{2}^{H}=1\},

see Figure 3(i)(i).

Analogously, the information within ℱ2≤\mathcal{F}_{2}^{\leq} is completely determined if we specify the polygonal subdivision ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} of 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P}, obtained by considering the sets of the form

(−Ci)∩𝒟2P(-C_{i})\cap\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P}

for all the cones Ci∈ℱ2≤C_{i}\in\mathcal{F}_{2}^{\leq}, where3737 37 For simplicity, when we draw the set 𝒟1P\mathscr{D}_{1}^{P}, we will show it as a 1D set within the X2PX_{2}^{P}-space, automatically understood to lie within the subset of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} where the first coordinate X1PX_{1}^{P} is 1, see Figure 3(k)(k) (and compare it with Figure 3(j)(j)).

𝒟1P=compactification⁡({(1,X2P)∈ℝ≥02|1≤X2P}),\mathscr{D}_{1}^{P}={\rm compactification}(\{(1,X_{2}^{P})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{\geq 0}|1\leq X_{2}^{P}\}),

see Figure 3(j)(j). Note that the point at infinity is shown in Figure 3(j)(j) as the red point with orange center.

Equivalently, we can define the elements of ℱ1H\mathcal{F}_{1}^{H} as the images of the elements of ℱ2≤\mathcal{F}_{2}^{\leq} (except for the zero vector) via the transformation ψ2H\psi_{2}^{H} given by

ψ2H​(X1,X2)=(X1X1+X2,X2X1+X2),\psi_{2}^{H}(X_{1},X_{2})=\left(\frac{X_{1}}{X_{1}+X_{2}},\frac{X_{2}}{X_{1}+X_{2}}\right),

and we can define the elements of ℱ1P\mathcal{F}_{1}^{P} as the images of the elements of ℱ2≥\mathcal{F}_{2}^{\geq} via the transformation ψ2P\psi_{2}^{P} given by3939 39 In the case of ψ2P\psi_{2}^{P} we allow division by zero when X1=0X_{1}=0, and then the point at infinity belongs to the image of ψ2P\psi_{2}^{P}.

Remark. Since we have compactified 𝒟1P\mathscr{D}_{1}^{P} with a point at infinity, it follows that the two transformations ψ2H\psi_{2}^{H} and ψ2P\psi_{2}^{P} described above become homeomorphisms from 𝒟1P\mathscr{D}_{1}^{P} to 𝒟1H\mathscr{D}_{1}^{H}, and from 𝒟1H\mathscr{D}_{1}^{H} to 𝒟1P\mathscr{D}_{1}^{P}, respectively. This fact gives another way to think about our compactification of 𝒟1P\mathscr{D}_{1}^{P}: it is the compactification of the set {(1,X2P)∈ℝ≥02|1≤X2P}\{(1,X_{2}^{P})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{\geq 0}|1\leq X_{2}^{P}\} for which

ψ2P:𝒟1H→𝒟1P\psi_{2}^{P}:\mathscr{D}_{1}^{H}\to\mathscr{D}_{1}^{P}

is a homeomorphism. ∎

Let us now explain how one can take advantage of the subdivision ℱ1P\mathcal{F}_{1}^{P} of 𝒟1P\mathcal{D}_{1}^{P} to construct a ZSH for ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2}.

The first step (see Figure 3(k)(k)) is to construct one more subdivision, with intervals TiT_{i}, as shown in Figure 3(k)(k). Note that each interval TiT_{i} contains exactly one red point (the red points are elements of ℱ1P\mathcal{F}_{1}^{P}). The red point inside TiT_{i} is called the basepoint of TiT_{i}. For example, using the notation from Figure 3(k)(k) the point Q0Q_{0} is the basepoint of T1T_{1}, BiB_{i} is the basepoint of TiT_{i} for 2≤i≤52\leq i\leq 5, and the point Q∞Q_{\infty} (which is the point at infinity of 𝒟1P\mathcal{D}_{1}^{P}) is the basepoint of T6T_{6}.

The subdivision with intervals TiT_{i} is called a ZSH blueprint of ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2}, and each interval TiT_{i} is called a tile of the ZSH blueprint.

Once we have the ZSH blueprint (which contains information about all the tiles and their basepoints) we will see that this is sufficient information in order to construct a ZSH. More precisely, we will impose that each edge of the ZSH maps to a tile of the ZSH blueprint via the map

Ψ2​(X1,X2)=(1,log⁡X2log⁡X1),\Psi_{2}(X_{1},X_{2})=\left(1,\ \frac{\log X_{2}}{\log X_{1}}\right),

and moreover each edge is orthogonal to the basepoint of its corresponding tile.

Recall that we plan to construct only the “half” of the ZSH that lies below the line {x1=x2}\{x_{1}=x_{2}\}, because we can then obtain the other half by symmetry.

Let us now start the construction of a ZSH (like the one shown in Figure 3(h)(h)) by choosing first the point P0P_{0} of the ZSH that lies on the line {x1=x2}\{x_{1}=x_{2}\}, say the point of coordinates (ε,ε)(\varepsilon,\varepsilon) for some very small number ε>0\varepsilon>0. Note that we have

Ψ2​(P0)=Q0,\Psi_{2}(P_{0})=Q_{0},

which is the left-side endpoint of the tile T1T_{1}. Then we proceed as follows. The first line segment of the ZSH we are constructing starts at the point P0P_{0} and goes below the line {x1=x2}\{x_{1}=x_{2}\} in a direction orthogonal to the basepoint of T1T_{1}, until it reaches a point P12P_{12} such that

Ψ2​(P12)=Q12,\Psi_{2}(P_{12})=Q_{12},

which is the right-side endpoint of the tile T1T_{1}.

The next line segment of the ZSH will start at the point P12P_{12} and go in a direction4040 40 Strictly speaking, there are two directions that start at the point P12P_{12} and go orthogonal to the basepoint of T2T_{2}, and there is an angle of 180o180^{o} between them. We choose the one that can result in a point P23P_{23} such that Ψ2​(P23)=Q23\Psi_{2}(P_{23})=Q_{23}, i.e., the one where X2PX_{2}^{P} increases along the edge. orthogonal to the basepoint of T2T_{2}, until it reaches a point P23P_{23} such that

Ψ2​(P23)=Q23,\Psi_{2}(P_{23})=Q_{23},

which is the right-side endpoint of the tile T2T_{2}.

We continue similarly until we reach the point P56P_{56} such that

Ψ2​(P56)=Q56,\Psi_{2}(P_{56})=Q_{56},

which is the right-side endpoint of the tile T5T_{5}.

Finally, the last edge of our ZSH starts at P56P_{56} and goes in a direction orthogonal to the basepoint of T6T_{6}; but the basepoint of T6T_{6} is the point at infinity denoted Q∞Q_{\infty}, which means that this last edge must be perfectly horizontal4141 41 Because, informally speaking, the coordinates of Q∞Q_{\infty} in 𝒟1P\mathcal{D}_{1}^{P} are (1,∞)(1,\infty). If we want to avoid dealing with “∞\infty” we can use the version of Q∞Q_{\infty} from 𝒟1H\mathcal{D}_{1}^{H} (see Figure 3(i)(i)) instead of the Q∞Q_{\infty} from 𝒟1P\mathcal{D}_{1}^{P}; that one is simply the vector (0,1) so, of course, orthogonal to it means perfectly horizontal..

To see that we have indeed succeeded in constructing a ZSH we claim now that we are in the setting of Lemma 9.7, i.e., for any nonzero cone 𝒞\mathcal{C} in ℱ2≤\mathcal{F}_{2}^{\leq}, the polygonal curve we have constructed above has the property that there exists a cone K𝒞K_{\mathcal{C}} such that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is contained in the interior of K𝒞K_{\mathcal{C}} and such that for any point PP of the ZSH such that log⁡(P)\log(P) belongs to K𝒞K_{\mathcal{C}} we have that the outer normal of the ZSH at PP belongs to 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Indeed, if 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a one-dimensional cone in ℱ2≤\mathcal{F}_{2}^{\leq} then the image of 𝒞\mathcal{C} within 𝒟2P\mathcal{D}_{2}^{P} is the basepoint of a tile TiT_{i}. Then we can define K𝒞K_{\mathcal{C}} to be the two-dimensional cone that corresponds to the tile TiT_{i}. Also, consider the case where 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a two-dimensional cone in ℱ2≤\mathcal{F}_{2}^{\leq}. Then, regarded within 𝒟2P\mathcal{D}_{2}^{P}, the cone 𝒞\mathcal{C} “spans” two adjacent tiles, say TiT_{i} and Ti+1T_{i+1}, and we can define K𝒞K_{\mathcal{C}} to be the two-dimensional cone that corresponds to the union of the tiles TiT_{i} and Ti+1T_{i+1}.

Note also that we can choose the initial point (ε,ε)(\varepsilon,\varepsilon) to have an arbitrarily small ε\varepsilon. Therefore, we are indeed in the setting of Lemma 9.74242 42 Note that Lemma 9.7 only guarantees that our toric differential inclusion cannot cross our polygonal curve within the unit square (0,1)2(0,1)^{2}. Nevertheless, it is sufficient for our purposes, because this will remain true for a large enough distance outside the unit square (more precisely, until the curve reaches a new uncertainly region along one of the axes, which, if ε\varepsilon is small enough, will only happen for very large values of x1x_{1}), see Figure 3(e)(e)., which implies that our polygonal curve is a ZSH.

6 Proof of the global attractor conjecture in the three-dimensional case

We now discuss the construction of ZSH for three-dimensional toric differential inclusions.

For our construction of ZSH in ℝ>03\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{3} we will rely very heavily on two-dimensional representations of three-dimensional fans using subdivisions of the sets 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P} (and/or 𝒟2H\mathscr{D}_{2}^{H}) described below, and on the corresponding notion of two-dimensional ZSH blueprint.

Recall that in the previous section we have been able to use one-dimensional ZSH blueprints for the construction of one-dimensional ZSH in ℝ>02\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{2} (i.e., for the construction of polygonal curves that satisfy the ZSH property). Moreover, our construction was “canonical”, in the following sense: once we specified the starting point P0P_{0} of coordinates (ε,ε)(\varepsilon,\varepsilon), everything else was uniquely determined by the following simple conditions: (i)(i) the edges of the ZSH are in one-to-one correspondence with the tiles of the ZSH blueprint, (i​i)(ii) each edge is orthogonal to the basepoint of its corresponding tile, and (i​i​i)(iii) the image of each edge via the map Ψ2\Psi_{2} is exactly its corresponding tile.

In the next subsection we will choose an especially convenient fan ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3}, define a ZSH blueprint for it, and devise a construction process for the ZSH which is based on this ZSH blueprint. We will see that we have to adapt and modify some of the rules (i)(i)-(i​i​i)(iii) described above, but in the end we can create such a construction process, and to some extent it can also be seen as “canonical”, under somewhat relaxed restrictions. More precisely, our construction give rise to a polyhedral ZSH such that: (i′)(i^{\prime}) the faces of the ZSH are in one-to-one correspondence with the tiles of the ZSH blueprint, (i​i′)(ii^{\prime}) each face is orthogonal to the basepoint of its corresponding tile, and (i​i​i′)(iii^{\prime}) the image of each edge via the map Ψ3\Psi_{3} is arbitrarily close to its corresponding tile (in a sense that will be clarified below).

In a later subsection we will describe the construction of a polyhedral ZSH for a fully general choice of fan ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3}.

6.1 The proof in a special case

Similar to the previous section, we consider a fan ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} that is X1X_{1}-X2X_{2}-X3X_{3}-symmetric, and we assume4343 43 Recall that these assumptions can be made without loss of generality, because, if needed, we are just replacing ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} with a finer version of ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3}; any ZSH for the finer fan will also be a ZSH for the coarser fan. that all planes {Xi=Xj}\{X_{i}=X_{j}\} and {Xi=0}\{X_{i}=0\} can be realized as unions of cones that belong to ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3}. Recall that we only need to specify ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} within the negative orthant; moreover, due to symmetry, we only need to specify ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} within the subset of the negative orthant where we have X3≤X2≤X1≤0X_{3}\leq X_{2}\leq X_{1}\leq 0. Let us denote the restriction of ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} to this subset by ℱ3≤\mathcal{F}_{3}^{\leq} (here the superscript “≤\leq” is meant to remind us the inequality X3≤X2≤X1≤0X_{3}\leq X_{2}\leq X_{1}\leq 0). Then the part of ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} within the negative orthant is uniquely determined by ℱ3≤\mathcal{F}_{3}^{\leq}, and for now on we will focus on ℱ3≤\mathcal{F}_{3}^{\leq}.

Also similar to the previous section, the information within ℱ3≤\mathcal{F}_{3}^{\leq} is completely determined if we specify the polygonal subdivision4444 44 By polygonal subdivision (or simply subdivision) of 𝒟2H\mathscr{D}_{2}^{H} we mean a set of convex polygons, line segments, and points, which satisfies properties that are similar to the properties of a fan: any face of an element of the subdivision is also an element of the subdivision, and the intersection of two elements of the subdivision is a face of both. ℱ2H\mathcal{F}_{2}^{H} of 𝒟2H\mathscr{D}_{2}^{H}, obtained by considering the sets of the form

(−Ci)∩𝒟2H(-C_{i})\cap\mathscr{D}_{2}^{H}

for all the cones Ci∈ℱ3≤C_{i}\in\mathcal{F}_{3}^{\leq}, where

𝒟2H={(X1H,X2H,X3H)∈ℝ≥03|X1H≤X2H≤X3H​and​X1H+X2H+X3H=1}.\mathscr{D}_{2}^{H}=\{(X_{1}^{H},X_{2}^{H},X_{3}^{H})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}_{\geq 0}\ |\ X_{1}^{H}\leq X_{2}^{H}\leq X_{3}^{H}\mathrm{and}\ X_{1}^{H}+X_{2}^{H}+X_{3}^{H}=1\}.

Analogously, the information within ℱ3≤\mathcal{F}_{3}^{\leq} is completely determined if we specify the polygonal subdivision ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} of 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P}, obtained by considering the sets of the form

(−Ci)∩𝒟2P(-C_{i})\cap\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P}

Note that, equivalently, we can define the elements of ℱ2H\mathcal{F}_{2}^{H} as the images of the elements of ℱ3≤\mathcal{F}_{3}^{\leq} (except for the zero vector) via the transformation ψ3H\psi_{3}^{H} given by

ψ3H​(X1,X2,X3)=(X1X1+X2+X3,X2X1+X2+X3,X3X1+X2+X3),\psi_{3}^{H}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})=\left(\frac{X_{1}}{X_{1}+X_{2}+X_{3}},\frac{X_{2}}{X_{1}+X_{2}+X_{3}},\frac{X_{3}}{X_{1}+X_{2}+X_{3}}\right),

Remark. Since we have compactified 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P} with points at infinity, it follows that the two transformations ψ3H\psi_{3}^{H} and ψ3P\psi_{3}^{P} described above become homeomorphisms from 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P} to 𝒟2H\mathscr{D}_{2}^{H}, and from 𝒟2H\mathscr{D}_{2}^{H} to 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P}, respectively. This fact gives the simplest way to understand clearly our compactification of 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P}: it is the (unique) compactification of the set {(1,X2P,X3P)∈ℝ≥03|1≤X2P≤X3P}\{(1,X_{2}^{P},X_{3}^{P})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}_{\geq 0}|1\leq X_{2}^{P}\leq X_{3}^{P}\} for which

is a homeomorphism. ∎

6.1.1 Construction of a ZSH blueprint ℬ⁡(ℱ2P)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}) for a conveniently chosen ℱ3≤\mathcal{F}_{3}^{\leq}

For the sake of simplicity, let us now assume that ℱ3≤\mathcal{F}_{3}^{\leq} gives rise to the ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} which is exactly the subdivision of 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P} that is shown in Figure 4(a)(a). We have chosen this particular fan because we can now quickly build our key tool for the construction of a ZSH, i.e., a ZSH blueprint associated to the subdivision ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}. Indeed, a ZSH blueprint is shown (together with ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}) in Figure 4(b)(b) with blue lines; and the same ZSH blueprint is shown (without ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}) in Figure 4(c)(c).

Let us now clarify the notion of ZSH blueprint for this example. In general, given a subdivision ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} of 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P}, a ZSH blueprint ℬ⁡(ℱ2P)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}) is another subdivision of 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P} into quadrilateral “tiles”, together with the choice of a preferred point within each tile, called the “basepoint” of the tile, which satisfies several additional properties. To obtain the ZSH blueprint shown in Figure 4(b)(b) we have done the following:

Step 1. We created the blue box shown with thick blue dashed lines in Figure 4(d)(d), such that all the bounded4949 49 ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} also has two “unbounded vertices”, i.e., vertices that lie at infinity; these will be addressed in Step 4. vertices of ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} (i.e., the nine red dots) are contained in the interior of this blue box. 6.1.2 The use of the ZSH blueprint ℬ⁡(ℱ2P)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}) in the construction of the polyhedral surface 𝒫⁡(ℬ⁡(ℱ2P))\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}))

After we have constructed the ZSH blueprint ℬ⁡(ℱ2P)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}) shown in Figure 4(c)(c), we will use it for the construction of a polyhedral surface (denoted 𝒫⁡(ℬ⁡(ℱ2P))\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}))) within the set where 0<x3≤x2≤x1≤10<x_{3}\leq x_{2}\leq x_{1}\leq 1.

Later we will argue that, when we also take into account its symmetric images (and also extend it outside the unit cube, in a way that will also be specified later), the surface 𝒫⁡(ℬ⁡(ℱ2P))\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P})) will give rise to a ZSH for ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3}.

Our plan is that the polyhedral surface 𝒫⁡(ℬ⁡(ℱ2P))\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P})) will have 11 faces, which will be in a one-to-one correspondence with the tiles of ℬ⁡(ℱ2P)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}). Moreover, each face will be orthogonal to the basepoint of its corresponding tile. Even more, the image of each face via the map Ψ3P\Psi_{3}^{P} will approximate ‘‘arbitrarily closely”5050 50 We will see that, while for each face of the polyhedral surface 𝒫⁡(ℬ⁡(ℱ2P))\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P})) we can impose that it is exactly orthogonal to the basepoint of its corresponding tile, we cannot actually impose that the image of each face via Ψ3P\Psi_{3}^{P} is exactly the corresponding tile. Nevertheless, we can impose that this image approximates the corresponding tile as accurately as we want, and this will be sufficient for our goals. its corresponding tile (see Figure 5(e)(e) for an illustration of this approximation).

Before we start to describe the details of this construction, let us make the following general comment: while the construction of the polyhedral surface 𝒫⁡(ℬ⁡(ℱ2P))\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P})) takes place in ℝ>03\mathbb{R}^{3}_{>0}, we plan to observe our progress and collect information about construction rules by looking at the image via

of each piece of the surface while we are constructing it, and we will compare this image to the ZSH blueprint that we already have available to us within 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P}.

Let us “zoom-in” in the lower-left corner of Figure 4(c)(c), which is shown in Figure 5(a)(a).

Before we begin the construction of the faces FiF_{i}, let us first explain a very convenient abuse of terminology with respect to the tiles TiT_{i}. If a vertex QQ of a tile TiT_{i} lies on the boundary of another tile TjT_{j}, we will say that QQ is also a vertex of TjT_{j}. In other words, even though all tiles are actually quadrilaterals, we convene that some tiles may have more than four vertices (i.e., we regard some of these quadrilaterals as degenerate pentagons, or degenerate hexagons, etc., in the sense that some of their vertices are degenerate, i.e., the interior angle at such a vertex is exactly 180o180^{o}). For example, according to this convention, the tile T1T_{1} still has just four vertices, but the tile T4T_{4} has five vertices (because we convene that the point denoted Q124Q_{124} is a vertex of T4T_{4}). We also extend this abuse of terminology to edges, and we say that the tile T4T_{4} has five edges. (This unusual terminology will become very convenient soon, because it will allow us to say that each face FiF_{i} of the polyhedral surface 𝒫⁡(ℬ⁡(ℱ2P))\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P})) has the same number of vertices and the same number of edges as its corresponding tile TiT_{i}.)

Remark. Ideally, if it was possible, we would have liked to simply construct polygonal faces FiF_{i} of the polyhedral surface 𝒫⁡(ℬ⁡(ℱ2P))\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P})) such that

Ψ3P​(Fi)=Ti,\Psi_{3}^{P}(F_{i})=T_{i},

i.e., such that the “logarithmic projective image” of each face FiF_{i} is the tile TiT_{i}. Unfortunately, it turns out that this is impossible in 3D (although it was possible in 2D). Instead, we will make sure that the logarithmic projective image of each face FiF_{i} is a very good approximation of the tile TiT_{i}, i.e.,

Ψ3P​(Fi)≈Ti,\Psi_{3}^{P}(F_{i})\approx T_{i},

in a sense that will be clarified below. In particular, the vertices and edges of FiF_{i} will be in a ‘‘canonical” one-to-one correspondence with vertices and edges5151 51 Recall our unusual convention of what we consider to be vertices and edges of each TiT_{i}. of TiT_{i}, and the images via Ψ3P\Psi_{3}^{P} of vertices and edges of FiF_{i} can be made to lie arbitrarily closely to the corresponding vertices and edges of TiT_{i}. ∎
