In the next section we will consider the case of a fully general fan ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3}, and we will see that the construction of the ZSH blueprint within the blue box can become more complicated, and also that we will need to allow for any finite number of “tiles near infinity” (as opposed to just two such tiles in the special case of the fan ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} we used in this section). Nevertheless, a very similar approach will allow us to construct a ZSH in the general case.

6.2 The general construction of ZSH in 3D

In the previous section we have discussed the construction of ZSH in 3D for a convenient choice of polyhedral fan ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} (and corresponding subdivisions ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} and ℱ2H\mathcal{F}_{2}^{H}). We now consider the general case for ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3}.

Recall that ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} gives rise to two versions of ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2}, one (denoted ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}) within 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P} and another (denoted ℱ2H\mathcal{F}_{2}^{H}) within 𝒟2H\mathscr{D}_{2}^{H}. (Like before, without loss of generality, we assume that ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} is X1X_{1}-X2X_{2}-X3X_{3}-symmetric, and this ensures that all relevant information about ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} is contained in ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}, and also in ℱ2H\mathcal{F}_{2}^{H}.) Note also that the information contained in ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} is equivalent to the information contained in ℱ2H\mathcal{F}_{2}^{H}.

Our strategy for the construction of ZSH will rely again on a finite partition of 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P} (and, equivalently 𝒟2H\mathscr{D}_{2}^{H}) using well-chosen quadrilateral “tiles” (most of these tiles will be rectangular, with the exception of tiles lying along the boundary of 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P}). Like in the previous section, our plan is to construct a ZSH that has exactly one face for each “tile”; we will refer to this partition into tiles as a “ZSH blueprint”. Once we have built a ZSH blueprint we will see that the construction of the ZSH can proceed in the same way as in the previous section.

6.2.1 Construction of ZSH blueprint in 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P} (for a general ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P})

Consider a given ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} in 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P}, as shown in Figure 8(a)(a). We can see that the ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} in Figure 8(a)(a) is much more complicated than the one we have shown in Figure 4(a)(a). In particular, we see that the affine half-lines present in ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} have four different slopes, as opposed to just 2 different slopes (zero & one) in Figure 4(a)(a). More importantly, in Figure 4 we have avoided triangular regions in ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}, while in Figure 8 there are many triangular regions in ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}.

To illustrate the difficulty introduced by the presence of triangular regions, and also the fact that we can overcome it, let us look at the simpler subdivision ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} shown in Figure 9(a)(a). There is no immediate analogue of the type of blueprint we constructed in the previous section for this ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}. Nevertheless, we can construct a blueprint for this ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} by proceeding step by step as illustrated in Figure 9.

The key idea for the construction of the ZSH blueprint shown in Figure 9(f)(f) (see also the “zoom-in” version in Figure 9(g)(g)) is to do it in two stages: first choose a small enough6767 67 Here “small enough” means that we need to be able to accommodate the small blue vertical line segments, such that each blue vertical line segment intersects only one black line, i.e., intersects only the tile edge that it is orthogonal on. height for the blue horizontal strips that cover the horizontal half-lines of ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}, and partition them into quadrilaterals (one for each zero-dimensional element of ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}); then, choose an even smaller6868 68 The “even smaller” height needs to allow us to accommodate the small orange vertical line segments, such that each orange vertical line segment intersects no black line, i.e., intersects no tile edge. height for the orange horizontal strips, in order to be able to partition these orange strips into quadrilaterals as shown, with each quadrilateral intersecting exactly one one-dimensional element of ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}. Also, we choose the basepoints of these orange quadrilaterals to lie on this one-dimensional element of ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}, at a height that is exactly along the midline of each horizontal orange strip, as shown in Figure 9(g)(g). (A fully general discussion of the existence of such a blueprint for any fan ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} in ℝ>03\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{3}, and also for any fan ℱn\mathcal{F}_{n} in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} will be given in Section 7.)

Let us now also discuss the tiles that lie outside the blue box. We return to the larger fan ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} (and its corresponding ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}, shown in Figure 8(b)(b), since it better illustrates the general case, see Figure 10).

More specifically, in Figure 10(a)(a) we are ignoring what happened inside the blue box, and focus on the elements of ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} outside the blue box. Then, we construct one “boundary tile” for each slope featured by one such affine half-line element of ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}. Similar to the construction in the previous section, we choose the slopes of the three unbounded dotted blue lines (which separate the boundary tiles) such that their support lines pass through the origin (0,0)(0,0)6969 69 Recall from the previous section that images via Ψ3P\Psi_{3}^{P} of lines that are parallel to the x1x_{1}-axis are lines that pass through the origin. Therefore, this particular choice for the three unbounded dotted blue lines will be compatible later with our construction of the ZSH faces that correspond to boundary tiles as part of a cylindrical surface whose generating direction is the direction of the x1x_{1}-axis.. Also, the basepoint of each boundary tile lies at infinity, and represents the (common) slope of the black half-lines that are contained within that tile7070 70 The reason we have four tiles in Figure 10(a)(a) is that there are four different such slopes for half-lines of ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}..

The same four boundary tiles can be seen in Figure 10(b)(b). Note that now the four basepoints lie within the plane {X1H=0}\{X_{1}^{H}=0\}.

6.2.2 The use the ZSH blueprint in the construction of the ZSH

In general, once we have a ZSH blueprint as described in Figure 9 and Figure 10, the construction of the polyhedral ZSH is analogous to the construction described in the previous section.

For faces of the ZSH that correspond to tiles that lie inside the blue box the construction is completely similar. (Note that, like in the previous section, we have ensured that pairs of tiles that are adjacent horizontally satisfy the important property that their basepoints lie on the same horizontal line. This implies that any nonzero vector v=(v1,v2,v3)v=(v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}) that is orthogonal to two such basepoints must have v3=0v_{3}=0. This allows us to apply Lemma 9.10(i​i)(ii) to conclude that for any edge ee shared by such a pair of tiles its corresponding edge e^\hat{e} within the ZSH satisfies the property that Ψ3P​(e^)\Psi_{3}^{P}(\hat{e}) will be arbitrarily close7171 71 The most important information that we derive from Lemma 9.10(i​i)(ii) is that the tangent direction to any point of Ψ3P​(e^)\Psi_{3}^{P}(\hat{e}) is very close to vertical. to ee if ε0\varepsilon_{0} is small enough.)

For faces of the ZSH that correspond to tiles that lie outside the blue box the construction is also similar (i.e., we just build the cylindrical surface that starts along the outer edges of the blue box (when seen in 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P}) and uses the direction of the x1x_{1}-axis as its generator). On the other hand, the setting in Section 3 was simpler, with only two such “boundary tiles”, so we will look again at the representation of ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} in 𝒟2H\mathscr{D}_{2}^{H} (beside its representation in 𝒟2P\mathscr{D}_{2}^{P}) in order to understand precisely these boundary faces.

When we look at the four boundary tiles in 𝒟2H\mathscr{D}_{2}^{H} we can see that each one has a well defined basepoint (which specifies the normal of the corresponding face of the ZSH) and that these basepoints lie on the plane {X1=0}\{X_{1}=0\}, which confirms the fact that each one of these four “outer faces” are supported by planes that are parallel to the x1x_{1}-axis.

The fact that the polyhedral surface 𝒫⁡(ℬ⁡(ℱ2P))\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P})) discussed in this section is indeed a ZSH (and that 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} cannot cross this ZSH within any cube [0,M]3[0,M]^{3} if we choose ε\varepsilon small enough) can be argued exactly like in the previous section7272 72 Some of the key observations 1-3 about images of faces of 𝒫⁡(ℬ⁡(ℱ2P))\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P})) need to be modified slightly. For example, in observation “2.” for some edges ee of the subdivision ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} there are more than two tiles whose basepoints lie on ee (and these basepoints are not necessarily endpoints of ee), so we need to use a union of faces that correspond to these tiles, but this does not change anything relevant in the proof. Also, in observation “3.” it is no longer true that any face ff of ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} can be covered with just three or four tiles of ℬ⁡(ℱ2P)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}), but this also does not change anything relevant in the proof..

7 Subdivisions in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, their ZSH pre-blueprints, and their faithful ZSH blueprints

We have already seen that key properties of 3D toric differential inclusion 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} can be represented by a 2D subdivision ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} that is obtained from the 3D polyhedral fan ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} of 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3}. Also, we have seen how a 2D ZSH blueprint ℬ⁡(ℱ2P)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}) can be used for constructing a ZSH in 3D.

Here we will extend this approach to nnD, while also modifying the 2D construction accordingly, in order to be able to include it in the framework of an induction on dimension.

For example, the general 2D subdivisions that we consider here are no longer restricted to the subset 𝒟2P⊂ℝ2\mathcal{D}_{2}^{P}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}, see Figure 11(a)(a); similarly, in this section nnD subdivisions will be defined on the whole ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, instead of being restricted to a subset of it.

Moreover, instead of just ZSH blueprints, we will also discuss ZSH pre-blueprints, and use them as a key tool for constructing faithful ZSH blueprints, which will play an especially important role here. Also, in this section these pre-blueprints and blueprints will be defined on the whole Euclidean space (i.e., they will not be restricted to a subset of it, as in Section 6).

See Figure 11(b)(b) for an example of a ZSH pre-blueprint, and see Figure 14(g)(g) for an illustration of a faithful ZSH blueprint.

7.1 Polyhedral fans and subdivisions in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}

Recall that by a “fan” we mean a complete and pointed polyhedral fan. We start by defining a special kind of fan, called x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-fan. The definition proceeds inductively, for all n≥2n\geq 2, as follows.

An x1x_{1}-x2x_{2}-fan ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} is a fan in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} that contains both of the 1D cones (i.e., rays) that lie along the x2x_{2}-axis.

An x1x_{1}-x3x_{3}-fan ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} is a fan in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} such that there exists a x1x_{1}-x2x_{2}-fan ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} with the property that π3​(ℱ3)=ℱ2\pi_{3}(\mathcal{F}_{3})=\mathcal{F}_{2}, where π3\pi_{3} is the standard projection from ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} to ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. This means that, in particular, the half-planes in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} that project to rays of ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} must be unions of cones of ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3}. Also, the set π3−1​({0})\pi_{3}^{-1}(\{0\}), i.e., the x3x_{3}-axis, must be a union of cones of ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3}, namely the positive ray and the negative ray of the x3x_{3}-axis7373 73 Note that we could have also defined an “x1x_{1}-x1x_{1}-fan” to be any fan in ℝ1\mathbb{R}^{1}, and then an equivalent definition of an x1x_{1}-x2x_{2}-fan could have been a fan ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} such that there exists a x1x_{1}-x1x_{1}-fan ℱ1\mathcal{F}_{1} in ℝ1\mathbb{R}^{1} such that π2​(ℱ2)=ℱ1\pi_{2}(\mathcal{F}_{2})=\mathcal{F}_{1}, i.e., would have been analogous to the definition of an x1x_{1}-x3x_{3}-fan. (By the way, note also that there exists actually only one fan in ℝ1\mathbb{R}^{1}, because we only consider complete fans.).

Similarly, in general, a x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-fan ℱn\mathcal{F}_{n} is a fan in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} such that there exists a x1x_{1}-xn−1x_{n-1}-fan ℱn−1\mathcal{F}_{n-1} in ℝn−1\mathbb{R}^{n-1} with the property that πn​(ℱn)=ℱn−1\pi_{n}(\mathcal{F}_{n})=\mathcal{F}_{n-1}.

We will now define some polyhedral subdivisions of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} called x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivisions, which are strongly related to x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-fans. Consider the embedding

in:ℝn→ℝn+1i_{n}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n+1}

obtained by mapping ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} to the hyperplane {x1=1}\{x_{1}=1\} in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1} via

in​(x1,…,xn)=(1,x1,…,xn).i_{n}(x_{1},...,x_{n})=(1,x_{1},...,x_{n}).

Then an x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivision 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} is a polyhedral subdivision of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} that can be obtained by using the embedding ini_{n} to identify ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with the hyperplane {x1=1}\{x_{1}=1\} of ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, and then taking the intersection of this hyperplane with all the cones of a x1x_{1}-xn+1x_{n+1}-fan ℱn+1\mathcal{F}_{n+1}. In other words, up to the identification given by ini_{n}, we have

𝒮n={C∩{x1=1}|C∈ℱn+1}.\mathcal{S}_{n}=\{C\cap\{x_{1}=1\}\ |\ C\in\mathcal{F}_{n+1}\}.

In particular, note that this implies that for any x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivision 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} there exists an x1x_{1}-xn−1x_{n-1}-subdivision 𝒮n−1\mathcal{S}_{n-1} such that πn​(𝒮n)=𝒮n−1\pi_{n}(\mathcal{S}_{n})=\mathcal{S}_{n-1}.

An element of an x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivision 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} is called a face of 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n}, i.e., up to the identification given by ini_{n}, a face of 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} is a nonempty intersection between some cone C∈ℱn+1C\in\mathcal{F}_{n+1} and the plane {x1=1}\{x_{1}=1\}.

In subsection 7.3 will define ZSH pre-blueprints for any x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivision 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n}, and in subsection 7.4 we will use ZSH pre-blueprints in order to define faithful ZSH blueprints for any x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivision 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n}.

7.2 Binary words for faces of an x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivision 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n}

Consider an x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivision 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n}. First, note that to any face Δ0∈𝒮n\Delta_{0}\in\mathcal{S}_{n} we can associate a binary word of length nn denoted

α⁡(Δ0)=α1​a2​…​an¯∈{0,1}n,\alpha(\Delta_{0})=\overline{\alpha_{1}a_{2}...a_{n}}\in\{0,1\}^{n},

as follows. Consider the face πn​(Δ0)\pi_{n}(\Delta_{0}) in ℝn−1\mathbb{R}^{n-1}; if we have

dim(πn​(Δ0))=dim(Δ0)\dim(\pi_{n}(\Delta_{0}))=\dim(\Delta_{0})

then we define αn=0\alpha_{n}=0, and if

dim(πn​(Δ0))=dim(Δ0)−1\dim(\pi_{n}(\Delta_{0}))=\dim(\Delta_{0})-1

then we define αn=1\alpha_{n}=1. Similarly, we define

αn−1=dim(πn​(Δ0))−dim(πn−1​(πn​(Δ0))),\alpha_{n-1}=\dim(\pi_{n}(\Delta_{0}))-\dim(\pi_{n-1}(\pi_{n}(\Delta_{0}))),

and so on. In other words, as we consider the successive projections πn\pi_{n}, πn−1\pi_{n-1}, πn−2,…,π1\pi_{n-2},...,\pi_{1} of Δ0\Delta_{0}, the binary letter αj\alpha_{j} tells us if the jthj^{\mathrm{th}} projection πj\pi_{j} did or did not cause its dimension to decrease by one unit. Equivalently, but in the opposite order, we can think about Δ0\Delta_{0} as having been “grown” by starting from a single point 0∈ℝ00\in\mathbb{R}^{0}, and then its dimension went up by one unit at every stage jj that has αj=1\alpha_{j}=1.

7.3 ZSH pre-blueprints of an x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivision 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n}

In this subsection we introduce and study the notion of ZSH pre-blueprint associated to an x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivision 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n}. Our main goal in this section is to show that we can construct ZSH blueprints for 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n}, and the construction of ZSH pre-blueprints in this subsection will be the most important step towards that goal.

We first define one-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprints; these are sets of intervals with disjoint interiors that cover ℝ1\mathbb{R}^{1} and have a strong relationship with a given x1x_{1}-x1x_{1}-subdivision. Consider an x1x_{1}-x1x_{1}-subdivision 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}, as shown in Figure 12. In general, 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} consists of a finite set of points (i.e., 0-faces) and a finite set of closed intervals (i.e., 1-faces) whose endpoints are those 0-faces.

A ZSH pre-blueprint of 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} is given by an assignment of a closed interval denoted 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma) for any σ∈𝒮1\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{1} such that there exists some positive number denoted ε⁡(0)\varepsilon(0) for which we have

𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ0)=σ0+[−ε⁡(0),ε⁡(0)]\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma_{0})=\sigma_{0}+[-\varepsilon(0),\varepsilon(0)]

for any 0-face σ0∈𝒮1\sigma_{0}\in\mathcal{S}_{1}, and

𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ1)=σ1∖⋃σ0∈𝒮1𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ0)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma_{1})=\sigma_{1}\setminus\displaystyle\bigcup_{\sigma_{0}\in\mathcal{S}_{1}}\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma_{0})

for any 1-face σ1∈𝒮1\sigma_{1}\in\mathcal{S}_{1} (where the union above is over 0-faces σ0∈𝒮1\sigma_{0}\in\mathcal{S}_{1}). Moreover, we require that ε⁡(0)\varepsilon(0) is small enough so the interiors of the intervals 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma) are disjoint for all σ∈𝒮1\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{1}.

More precisely, in general, a ZSH pre-blueprint ℬ1p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{1} of 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} as described above is defined as the set of intervals 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma), i.e., we have

ℬ1p={𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ)|σ∈𝒮1}.{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{1}=\{\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma)\ |\ \sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{1}\}.

Informally, we can think of “𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑\mathit{nbhd}” as a function that associates a subset of ℝ\mathbb{R} to any σ∈𝒮1\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{1}, according to the rules described above. Note then that the function 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑\mathit{nbhd} uniquely determines the set ℬ1p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{1}; also, less obviously, the set of intervals ℬ1p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{1} uniquely determines the function 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑\mathit{nbhd}. Indeed, given the set ℬ1p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{1} and some zero-dimensional σ0∈𝒮1\sigma_{0}\in\mathcal{S}_{1}, we can define 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ0)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma_{0}) to be the (unique) element of ℬ1p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{1} that contains the point σ0\sigma_{0}; and for any one-dimensional σ1∈𝒮1\sigma_{1}\in\mathcal{S}_{1}, we can define 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ1)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma_{1}) to be the (again, unique) element of ℬ1p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{1} that intersects σ1\sigma_{1} and was not already assigned to be the 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ0)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma_{0}) for some zero-dimensional σ0∈𝒮1\sigma_{0}\in\mathcal{S}_{1}.

We will now define two-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprints, i.e., ZSH pre-blueprints associated to x1x_{1}-x2x_{2}-subdivisions; these are composed of some special polygonal sets with disjoint interiors, which cover ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} and have a strong relationship with a given x1x_{1}-x2x_{2}-subdivision.

Consider an x1x_{1}-x2x_{2}-subdivision 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} that projects to an x1x_{1}-x1x_{1}-subdivision denoted 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}. We define a ZSH pre-blueprint ℬ2p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{2} of 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} as follows. First, we assume that we have already constructed a ZSH pre-blueprint ℬ1p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{1} of 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}, for some ε⁡(0)>0\varepsilon(0)>0 (on which additional restrictions will be imposed below).

Note now that there are four types of faces in 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2}, corresponding to the binary words 00, 01, 10, 11. Specifically, zero-dimensional faces σ00∈𝒮2\sigma_{00}\in\mathcal{S}_{2} have α⁡(σ00)=00\alpha(\sigma_{00})=00 and are just points in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}; one-dimensional faces σ01∈𝒮2\sigma_{01}\in\mathcal{S}_{2} with α⁡(σ01)=01\alpha(\sigma_{01})=01 are edges that are parallel to the x2x_{2}-axis; one-dimensional faces σ10∈𝒮2\sigma_{10}\in\mathcal{S}_{2} with α⁡(σ10)=10\alpha(\sigma_{10})=10 are edges that are not parallel to the x2x_{2}-axis; and, finally, two-dimensional faces σ11∈𝒮2\sigma_{11}\in\mathcal{S}_{2} with α⁡(σ11)=11\alpha(\sigma_{11})=11 are polygons7474 74 Some edges and some polygons are unbounded..

Consider some positive numbers ε⁡(00)\varepsilon(00) and ε⁡(10)\varepsilon(10) and define ε⁡(01)=ε⁡(0)\varepsilon(01)=\varepsilon(0). Informally, it will be convenient to assume that we have

0<ε⁡(10)≪ε⁡(01)≪ε⁡(00)≪1;0<\varepsilon(10)\ll\varepsilon(01)\ll\varepsilon(00)\ll 1;

this will be made more precise below.

As in the one-dimensional case, we will now define a set 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma) for any σ∈𝒮2\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{2}. Consider first a zero-dimensional face σ00∈𝒮2\sigma_{00}\in\mathcal{S}_{2}. We define

𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ00)=σ00+[−ε⁡(01),ε⁡(01)]×[−ε⁡(00),ε⁡(00)].\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma_{00})=\sigma_{00}+[-\varepsilon(01),\varepsilon(01)]\times[-\varepsilon(00),\varepsilon(00)].

If σ10∈𝒮2\sigma_{10}\in\mathcal{S}_{2} has α⁡(σ10)=10\alpha(\sigma_{10})=10 then we define

𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ10)=(σ10+[−ε⁡(10),ε⁡(10)])∩(𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(π2​(σ10))×ℝ).\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma_{10})=\left(\sigma_{10}+[-\varepsilon(10),\varepsilon(10)]\right)\mathbin{\scalebox{1.25}{$\cap$}}\left(\mathit{nbhd}(\pi_{2}(\sigma_{10}))\times\mathbb{R}\right).

For the faces of the form σ01\sigma_{01} and σ11\sigma_{11} (i.e., having corresponding binary words 01 and 11, respectively) we define their 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑\mathit{nbhd} by taking advantage of the ones already defined above. Specifically, for an edge σ01∈𝒮2\sigma_{01}\in\mathcal{S}_{2} we define 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ01)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma_{01}) to be the subset of

𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(π2​(σ01))×ℝ\mathit{nbhd}(\pi_{2}(\sigma_{01}))\times\mathbb{R}

that is delimited by 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ00′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime}_{00}) and 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ00′′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime\prime}_{00}), where σ00′\sigma^{\prime}_{00} and σ00′′\sigma^{\prime\prime}_{00} are the endpoints of σ01\sigma_{01}. (If σ01\sigma_{01} is unbounded then only one such delimiter is needed.)

The definition of 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ11)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma_{11}) for some triangle σ11∈𝒮2\sigma_{11}\in\mathcal{S}_{2} is similar, except that the delimiting points σ00′\sigma^{\prime}_{00} and σ00′′\sigma^{\prime\prime}_{00} are replaced by delimiting edges σ10′\sigma^{\prime}_{10} and σ10′′\sigma^{\prime\prime}_{10} that are of binary type 10 and lie on the boundary of σ11\sigma_{11}. (And again, if σ11\sigma_{11} is unbounded, then only one such delimiting edge is needed.)

Moreover, we impose the condition that the interiors of 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime}) and 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ′′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime\prime}) are disjoint for all σ′≠σ′′∈𝒮2\sigma^{\prime}\neq\sigma^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{2}. It is easy to see in 2D that (for a fixed x1x_{1}-x2x_{2}-subdivision 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2}) if we assume that if the positive number

max⁡{ε⁡(00),ε⁡(01)ε⁡(00),ε⁡(10)ε⁡(01)}\max\Bigl\{\varepsilon(00),\frac{\varepsilon(01)}{\varepsilon(00)},\frac{\varepsilon(10)}{\varepsilon(01)}\Bigr\}

Assume now that we have defined ZSH pre-blueprints for x1x_{1}-xn−1x_{n-1}-subdivisons; we will now define ZSH pre-blueprints of an x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivison 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n}.

𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑​(πn​(σ))×ℝ\mathit{nbhd}(\pi_{n}(\sigma))\times\mathbb{R}

that is delimited by7878 78 This step in the constructions assumes that 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime}) and 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ′′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime\prime}) have disjoint interiors, and therefore there is a well defined notion of “subset of 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑​(πn​(σ))×ℝ\mathit{nbhd}(\pi_{n}(\sigma))\times\mathbb{R} delimited by 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime}) and 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ′′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime\prime})”. Of course, it is not obvious that the construction of nn-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprints described above is always possible. The theorem below tells us that for well-chosen values of ε^​(α)\hat{\varepsilon}(\alpha) we can guarantee that this construction is possible.

In order to formulate this theorem, recall that we have discussed above the real-valued function ε^​(α)\hat{\varepsilon}(\alpha); based on such a function we define another real-valued function ε⁡(α)\varepsilon(\alpha), which is only defined for binary words α\alpha of length exactly nn, and is given by

ε⁡(α1​α2​…​αn−1​0)=ε^​(α1​α2​…​αn−1​0)\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}...\alpha_{n-1}0)=\hat{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}...\alpha_{n-1}0)

and

ε⁡(α1​α2​…​αk−1​011​…​1)=ε^​(α1​α2​…​αk−1​0).\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}...\alpha_{k-1}011...1)=\hat{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}...\alpha_{k-1}0).

In other words, the value of ε⁡(α)\varepsilon(\alpha) is the same as the value of ε^​(α^)\hat{\varepsilon}(\hat{\alpha}), where α^\hat{\alpha} is obtained from α\alpha by erasing all the “1” bits at the end of α\alpha. Note that, in particular, we have ε⁡(α)>0\varepsilon(\alpha)>0 for all8080 80 Except for the word 11…11, because ε⁡(11​…​11)\varepsilon(11...11) is not defined. binary words α\alpha of length nn.

Theorem 7.1.

Consider an x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivison 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} and some functions ε^​(α)\hat{\varepsilon}(\alpha) and ε⁡(α)\varepsilon(\alpha) as described above. If the number

ε(pℬn):=max{ε(00…00),ε⁡(00​…​01)ε⁡(00​…​00),ε⁡(00​…​10)ε⁡(00​…​01),…,ε⁡(11​…​10)ε⁡(11​…​01)}\varepsilon(^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{n}):=\max\Bigl\{\varepsilon(00...00),\frac{\varepsilon(00...01)}{\varepsilon(00...00)},\frac{\varepsilon(00...10)}{\varepsilon(00...01)},...,\frac{\varepsilon(11...10)}{\varepsilon(11...01)}\Bigr\} (12)

is small enough8181 81 Note that this is essentially equivalent to saying that we have ε⁡(11​…​10)≪ε⁡(11​…​01)≪…≪ε⁡(00​…​10)≪ε⁡(00​…​01)≪ε⁡(00​…​00)≪1\varepsilon(11...10)\ll\varepsilon(11...01)\ll...\ll\varepsilon(00...10)\ll\varepsilon(00...01)\ll\varepsilon(00...00)\ll 1, and therefore the magnitude sizes of the numbers ε⁡(α)\varepsilon(\alpha) grow exactly in the opposite direction than the standard ordering of the binary numbers given by the binary words α\alpha., then the construction of a ZSH pre-blueprint ℬnp{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{n} of 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} described above is well defined. In particular, if σ′≠σ′′∈𝒮n\sigma^{\prime}\neq\sigma^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{n}, then the interiors of 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime}) and 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ′′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime\prime}) are disjoint.

Proof.

We proceed by induction, so we assume that we already know this to be true in dimensions ≤n−1\leq n-1.

Note that if we can impose some upper bound on the quantity shown in (12), then we can also impose the same upper bound on the corresponding quantity that is restricted only to binary words α\alpha of the form α1​α2​…​αn−1​1\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}...\alpha_{n-1}1, and these can be regarded as nbhd sizes for ZSH pre-blueprints constructed for the projections of 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} in dimensions 1, 2, …, n−1n-1.

Then, if the quantity in (12) is small enough, we can apply the induction hypothesis to the ZSH pre-blueprint of πn​(𝒮n)\pi_{n}(\mathcal{S}_{n}) that appears in the definition of ℬnp{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{n}, and it follows that the interiors of 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(πn​(σ′))\mathit{nbhd}(\pi_{n}(\sigma^{\prime})) and 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(πn​(σ′′))\mathit{nbhd}(\pi_{n}(\sigma^{\prime\prime})) are disjoint for all σ′,σ′′∈𝒮n\sigma^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{n} such that πn​(σ′)≠πn​(σ′′)\pi_{n}(\sigma^{\prime})\neq\pi_{n}(\sigma^{\prime\prime}), and therefore the interiors of 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime}) and 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ′′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime\prime}) are also disjoint for all σ′,σ′′∈𝒮n\sigma^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{n} such that πn​(σ′)≠πn​(σ′′)\pi_{n}(\sigma^{\prime})\neq\pi_{n}(\sigma^{\prime\prime}).

Therefore, it is now sufficient to show that 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime}) and 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ′′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime\prime}) are disjoint for those σ′,σ′′∈𝒮n\sigma^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{n} such that πn​(σ′)=πn​(σ′′)\pi_{n}(\sigma^{\prime})=\pi_{n}(\sigma^{\prime\prime}). Moreover, it is sufficient to consider the case where σ′\sigma^{\prime} and σ′′\sigma^{\prime\prime} have binary type α\alpha of the form α1​α2​…​αn−1​0\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}...\alpha_{n-1}08282 82 Because, once we have handled this case, in the other cases (i.e., both of the form α1​α2​…​αn−1​1\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}...\alpha_{n-1}1, or one of the form α1​α2​…​αn−1​0\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}...\alpha_{n-1}0 and the other of the form α1​α2​…​αn−1​1\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}...\alpha_{n-1}1), the interiors of 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime}) and 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ′′)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma^{\prime\prime}) are disjoint by definition.; in particular, we then have dim(σ′)=dim(σ′′)\dim(\sigma^{\prime})=\dim(\sigma^{\prime\prime}).

7.4 From ZSH pre-blueprints to faithful ZSH blueprints

In the previous section we have discussed the construction of ZSH pre-blueprints of an x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivision 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} for any nn. On the other hand, our ultimate goal is actually construction of ZSH, which requires a ZSH blueprint of 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n}. Here we discuss how we can use ZSH pre-blueprints in order to construct associated faithful ZSH blueprints, and why these are useful.

A faithful ZSH blueprint ℬn𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{n}^{\mathit{ff}} of 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} is a special kind of ZSH blueprint, which is strongly related to a given pre-blueprint ℬnp{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{n} of 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n}. In particular, for each σ∈𝒮n\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{n}, if we denote by ff-𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma) the union of all the tiles TnT_{n} of ℬn𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{n}^{\mathit{ff}} such that the basepoint of TnT_{n} belongs to σ\sigma, then ff-𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma) can approximate the set 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma) of ℬnp{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{n} arbitrarily well, in a sense that will be clarified below (see Figure 14 for an illustration).

More importantly, an nn-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint can be used for the construction of an (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional ZSH blueprint. Moreover, given enough additional information8686 86 We will see that this additional information will come from properties of an (n+2)(n+2)-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprint. This is not a problem, because we already know how to construct ZSH pre-blueprints in any dimension. (in a sense that will be discussed below), an nn-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint can be used for the construction of an (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint. Therefore, we will see that the use of faithful ZSH blueprints will allow us to construct ZSH blueprints in any dimension.

7.4.1 The one-dimensional case

We define a one-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint of a one-dimensional x1x_{1}-x1x_{1}-subdivision 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} as being obtained from a one-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprint8787 87 Note that a one-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprint is actually also a one-dimensional ZSH blueprint. ℬ1p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{1} of 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} as follows. We assume that we already are given an x1x_{1}-x2x_{2}-subdivision 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} such that 𝒮1=π2​(𝒮2)\mathcal{S}_{1}=\pi_{2}(\mathcal{S}_{2}), and a two-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprint ℬ2p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{2} of 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} such that ℬ1p=π2(pℬ2){}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{1}=\pi_{2}(^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{2})8888 88 It is important to note that, by definition, we cannot just look at a one-dimensional ZSH blueprint of 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} in isolation and say whether it is “faithful” or not. The property of being “faithful” depends on relationships between this one-dimensional ZSH blueprint of 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} and some two-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprint of 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2}.. Let us fix a number denoted ε~​(1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(1), which satisfies8989 89 Note that ε~​(1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(1) depends on ε⁡(10)\varepsilon(10), and the information about ε⁡(10)\varepsilon(10) comes from ℬ2p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{2}. Also, here is the precise meaning of the informal-looking condition “ε~​(1)≪ε​(10)\tilde{\varepsilon}(1)\ll\varepsilon(10)”: we mean that, once we are given the 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} and ℬ2p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{2}, then there exists some ε~0∈(0,ε⁡(10))\tilde{\varepsilon}_{0}\in(0,\varepsilon(10)) which depends only on 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} and ℬ2p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{2}, such that if we have ε~​(1)<ε~0\tilde{\varepsilon}(1)<\tilde{\varepsilon}_{0}, then we say that we have ε~​(1)≪ε​(10)\tilde{\varepsilon}(1)\ll\varepsilon(10).

ε~​(1)≪ε​(10).\tilde{\varepsilon}(1)\ll\varepsilon(10).

For each σ∈𝒮1\sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{1} such that ε⁡(σ)=1\varepsilon(\sigma)=1 we divide the interval 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma) into very small intervals of equal size, and this size is ≤ε~​(1)\leq\tilde{\varepsilon}(1), and as close to ε~​(1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(1) as possible9090 90 Since we have ε~​(1)≪1\tilde{\varepsilon}(1)\ll 1, and the length of any interval 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma) considered above is O⁡(1)O(1), it follows that the size of these small intervals is guaranteed to be very close to ε~​(1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(1). Note that we cannot guarantee their size to be exactly ε~​(1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(1), because we don’t know that this number is an integer factor of the length of 𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma).. The basepoints of all these new intervals are defined to be their centerpoints.

Some of the main ideas on how to construct a faithful ZSH blueprint in the two-dimensional case are illustrated in Figure 14.

We will write down all these conditions systematically, by imposing for each such binary type that we have

for each corresponding three-dimensional tile102102 102 The rigorous meaning of “≫\gg” here is similar to the previous case: we mean that there exists some ε~0<1\tilde{\varepsilon}_{0}<1 which depends only on 𝒮3\mathcal{S}_{3} and ℬ3p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{3}, such that we have ε~02​l​e​n​g​t​h>ε~0​w​i​d​t​h>h​e​i​g​h​t.\tilde{\varepsilon}_{0}^{2}\ length>\tilde{\varepsilon}_{0}\ width>height. This makes sense if we also note that we will use these order-of-magnitude conditions only in statements of the form “if ξ1≫ξ2\xi_{1}\gg\xi_{2} then…”, which is a short and convenient way of expressing the rigorous statement “there exists some ε~0<1\tilde{\varepsilon}_{0}<1 such that, if ε~0​ξ1>ξ2\tilde{\varepsilon}_{0}\xi_{1}>\xi_{2} then…”. .

Then the conditions are the following:

For​σ∈𝒮3​of​type​ 110:ε⁡(110)≫𝜺~​(𝟏𝟏)≫𝜺~​(𝟏)\displaystyle\mathrm{For}\ \sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{3}\ \mathrm{of\ type}\ 110:\ \ \varepsilon(110)\gg\boldsymbol{\tilde{\varepsilon}(11)}\gg\boldsymbol{\tilde{\varepsilon}(1)} (16)
For​σ∈𝒮3​of​type​ 100:ε⁡(100)≫ε⁡(10)≫𝜺~​(𝟏)\displaystyle\mathrm{For}\ \sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{3}\ \mathrm{of\ type}\ 100:\ \ \varepsilon(100)\gg\varepsilon(10)\ \gg\boldsymbol{\tilde{\varepsilon}(1)}
For​σ∈𝒮3​of​type​ 010:ε⁡(010)≫𝜺~​(𝟎𝟏)≫ε⁡(0)\displaystyle\mathrm{For}\ \sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{3}\ \mathrm{of\ type}\ 010:\ \ \varepsilon(010)\gg\boldsymbol{\tilde{\varepsilon}(01)}\gg\varepsilon(0)
For​σ∈𝒮3​of​type​ 000:ε⁡(000)≫ε⁡(00)≫ε⁡(0)\displaystyle\mathrm{For}\ \sigma\in\mathcal{S}_{3}\ \mathrm{of\ type}\ 000:\ \ \varepsilon(000)\gg\varepsilon(00)\ \gg\varepsilon(0)

Note that we have emphasized in (16) the new tile sizes ε~​(11)\tilde{\varepsilon}(11), ε~​(01)\tilde{\varepsilon}(01), and ε~​(1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(1) using bold fonts; all the other numbers in (16) are values of the form ε⁡(α)\varepsilon(\alpha) that come from the ZSH pre-blueprint ℬ3p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{3} of 𝒮3\mathcal{S}_{3}.

Let us make two observations about imposing the restrictions (16).

Our first observation is that these restrictions are already compatible with the properties of ℬ3p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{3}. Indeed, recall that for any nn-dimensional pre-blueprint ℬnp{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{n} we have

ε⁡(α1​…​αi)=ε⁡(α1​…​αi​11​…​1),\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i})=\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}11...1),

where the binary word α1​…​αi​11​…​1\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}11...1 has nn letters. Also recall that if α\alpha and β\beta are two binary words of nn letters which, regarded as binary numbers, satisfy α<β\alpha<\beta, then we have

ε⁡(α)≫ε⁡(β).\varepsilon(\alpha)\gg\varepsilon(\beta).

Therefore, if the binary word α1​…​αi\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i} is a strict prefix of a binary word of the form α1′​…​αj′​0\alpha_{1}^{\prime}...\alpha_{j}^{\prime}0, then we have

ε⁡(α1′​…​αj′​0)≫ε⁡(α1​…​αi),\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}^{\prime}...\alpha_{j}^{\prime}0)\gg\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}),

which are exactly the types of inequalities of the form ε⁡(α)≫ε⁡(β)\varepsilon(\alpha)\gg\varepsilon(\beta) that appear in (16).

Our second observation is that we can choose the new numbers ε~​(α)\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha) such that they satisfy the conditions (16). While this two-dimensional case is quite simple, a general way to do it (which works in the nn-dimensional case) is to proceed in two steps: in a first step define the new numbers ε~​(α1​…​αi​1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}1) such that the nn-dimensional analogue of (16) is almost satisfied, but some “≫\gg” are actually “==”; and in a second step modify all the numbers where we have “==” to obtain “≫\gg”, while the previously attained “≫\gg” still holds. This will be discussed in detail in the next subsection.

Let us also make one more remark: once we have chosen the numbers ε~​(1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(1), ε~​(01)\tilde{\varepsilon}(01), and ε~​(11)\tilde{\varepsilon}(11) such that they satisfy (16), here is how we use them. First, as we discussed in the previous subsection, the number ε~​(1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(1) will be used in the construction of the faithful ZSH blueprint ℬ1𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{1}^{\mathit{ff}} of 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1}. (Recall that we have used the number ε~​(1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(1) to specify (to an arbitrarily good approximation) the dimension along the x1x_{1}-axis of the tiles of ff-𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ1)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma_{1}), for any one-dimensional face σ1∈𝒮1\sigma_{1}\in\mathcal{S}_{1}.

Then the numbers ε~​(01)\tilde{\varepsilon}(01) and ε~​(11)\tilde{\varepsilon}(11) will be used in the construction of the faithful ZSH blueprint ℬ2𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{2}^{\mathit{ff}} of 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2}, as follows. The number ε~​(01)\tilde{\varepsilon}(01) will be used to specify the (approximate) dimension along the x2x_{2}-axis of the tiles of ff-𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ1)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma_{1}), for any one-dimensional face σ1∈𝒮2\sigma_{1}\in\mathcal{S}_{2} to binary type 01. Similarly, the number ε~​(11)\tilde{\varepsilon}(11) will be used to specify the (approximate) dimension along the x2x_{2}-axis of the tiles of ff-𝑛𝑏ℎ𝑑⁡(σ2)\mathit{nbhd}(\sigma_{2}), for any two-dimensional face σ2∈𝒮2\sigma_{2}\in\mathcal{S}_{2} to binary type 11.

Of course, as we have mentioned earlier, we could have done much less work in order to obtain just some ZSH blueprint ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} of 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2}. The key point here is that once we have a faithful ZSH blueprint ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} of 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2}, then, by definition, everything is “prearranged” to allow us to construct a ZSH blueprint ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{3} of 𝒮3\mathcal{S}_{3}, and most importantly, to construct a faithful ZSH blueprint ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{3} of 𝒮3\mathcal{S}_{3}, and therefore to keep this inductive process going and reach any desired dimension nn.

Note also that as the dimension increases we do actually impose additional conditions on the numbers ε~​(α1​…​αi​1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}1) which we have already used in previous construction steps. For example, when we wanted ℬ1𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{1}^{\mathit{ff}} to be faithful we imposed the restriction

ε​(10)≫ε~​(1),\varepsilon(10)\gg\tilde{\varepsilon}(1),

on ε~​(1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(1), but when we additionally wanted ℬ2𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{2}^{\mathit{ff}} to be faithful we imposed the additional restriction

ε​(110)≫ε~​(1)\varepsilon(110)\gg\tilde{\varepsilon}(1)

on ε~​(1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(1), which was not needed in order for ℬ1𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{1}^{\mathit{ff}} to be faithful, but was needed in order for ℬ2𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{2}^{\mathit{ff}} to be faithful. Therefore, we will see that there are different degrees of faithfulness, and in this case ℬ1𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{1}^{\mathit{ff}} is not just faithful, but it is 2-faithful103103 103 In general, if a kk-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint ℬk𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{k}^{\mathit{ff}} satisfies the conditions required for the construction (using the approach that we are discussing here) of an ℓ\ell-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint ℬℓ𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{\ell}^{\mathit{ff}} (with k<ℓk<\ell), then we say that ℬk𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{k}^{\mathit{ff}} is ℓ\ell-faithful. In other words, in order for ℬk𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{k}^{\mathit{ff}} to be ℓ\ell-faithful we have to check conditions similar to (16) up to dimension ℓ+1\ell+1. See the next subsection for more details..

7.4.3 The nn-dimensional case

In this subsection we discuss the general nn-dimensional case of our construction of a faithful ZSH blueprint ℬn𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{n}^{\mathit{ff}} for an x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivision 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n}. Our setting will be the following: we will assume that, for the x1x_{1}-xix_{i}-subdivisions 𝒮1,…,𝒮i,…,𝒮n,𝒮n+1\mathcal{S}_{1},...,\mathcal{S}_{i},...,\mathcal{S}_{n},\mathcal{S}_{n+1} we have already constructed a “chain” of ZHS pre-blueprints ℬ1p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{1}, ℬ2p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{2}, …, ℬnp{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{n}, ℬn+1p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{n+1}, and a “chain” of nn-faithful ZSH blueprints ℬ1𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{1}^{\mathit{ff}}, ℬ2𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{2}^{\mathit{ff}}, …, ℬn−1𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{n-1}^{\mathit{ff}} , respectively, where we have

𝒮i−1=πi(𝒮i),pℬi−1=πi(pℬi),ℬj−1𝑓𝑓=πj(ℬj𝑓𝑓),\mathcal{S}_{i-1}=\pi_{i}(\mathcal{S}_{i}),\ ^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{i-1}=\pi_{i}(^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{i}),\ \mathcal{B}_{j-1}^{\mathit{ff}}=\pi_{j}(\mathcal{B}_{j}^{\mathit{ff}}),

for all integers i,ji,j such that 2≤i≤n+12\leq i\leq n+1 and 2≤j≤n−12\leq j\leq n-1.

Remark. As we have mentioned in previous subsections, the reason we need faithful ZSH blueprints is the following. First of all, not every (n−1)(n-1)-dimensional ZSH blueprint ℬn−1\mathcal{B}_{n-1} of the x1x_{1}-xn−1x_{n-1}-subdivision 𝒮n−1=πn​(𝒮n)\mathcal{S}_{n-1}=\pi_{n}(\mathcal{S}_{n}) can serve as an induction hypothesis for the construction of a nn-dimensional ZSH blueprint ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} for the x1x_{1}-xnx_{n}-subdivision 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} such that ℬn−1=πn​(ℬn)\mathcal{B}_{n-1}=\pi_{n}(\mathcal{B}_{n}). On the other hand, if ℬn−1𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{n-1}^{\mathit{ff}} is an nn-faithful ZSH blueprint for 𝒮n−1\mathcal{S}_{n-1}, then not only can we build a ZSH blueprint ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} of 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} such that πn​(ℬn)=ℬn−1𝑓𝑓\pi_{n}(\mathcal{B}_{n})=\mathcal{B}_{n-1}^{\mathit{ff}}, but also104104 104 As we have seen in the previous subsection, for this second part we will need to impose some additional requirements, related to the (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional subdivision 𝒮n+1\mathcal{S}_{n+1}. We will discuss these additional requirements in this subsection, and we will make sure that they can be satisfied. we can build a faithful ZSH blueprint ℬn𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{n}^{\mathit{ff}} for 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} that is also based on ℬn−1𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{n-1}^{\mathit{ff}}. Therefore, since nn was arbitrary, we can extend this construction of faithful ZSH blueprints by induction.

Similar to the previous subsection, our construction will proceed in two steps. In Step 1 we will just construct a ZSH blueprint ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} for 𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{n} (not yet a faithful ZSH blueprint). Then, in Step 2, we will further refine our construction to obtain a faithful ZSH blueprint ℬn𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{n}^{\mathit{ff}}.

Before we start Step 1, let us first discuss the numbers ε~​(α)\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha) that will be needed in our construction, and their relationships to the numbers ε⁡(β)\varepsilon(\beta) that are provided to us by the previously constructed “chain” of ZHS pre-blueprints ℬ1p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{1}, ℬ2p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{2}, …, ℬnp{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{n}, ℬn+1p{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{n+1}.

Recall the conditions (16) we discussed in the previous subsection. It was not difficult to see that all these conditions can be enforced; on the other hand, in the nn-dimensional case we get 2n2^{n} such rows of conditions, and it is less clear that they can all be satisfied at the same time.

For example, for n=3n=3 here is what these 232^{3} conditions look like105105 105 Recall where these conditions are coming from: we want to construct ℬ3𝑓𝑓\mathcal{B}_{3}^{\mathit{ff}} which is a blueprint diagram for 𝒮3\mathcal{S}_{3}, and, moreover, can be used as “induction hypothesis” for the construction of a blueprint diagram ℬ4\mathcal{B}_{4} for 𝒮4\mathcal{S}_{4} such that π4​(ℬ4)=ℬ3𝑓𝑓\pi_{4}(\mathcal{B}_{4})=\mathcal{B}_{3}^{\mathit{ff}}. On the other hand, all these conditions simply say that, if we remove the last letter of a binary word α\alpha, then the corresponding epsilon value (i.e., ε⁡(α)\varepsilon(\alpha) or ε~​(α)\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha), depending on whether the last letter of α\alpha is 0 or 1, respectively106106 106 If the last letter of α\alpha is 0 then the value ε⁡(α)\varepsilon(\alpha) comes from the ZSH pre-blueprints pℬ1,pℬ2,,…,pℬn+1{}^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{1},^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{2},,...,^{p}\!\mathcal{B}_{n+1}. Therefore, in the general nn-dimensional case, all the inequalities that involve some ε~​(α)\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha) can be summarized simply as

ε⁡(α1​…​αj​011​…​10)≫ε~​(α1​…​αj​011​…​1)≫…≫ε~​(α1​…​αj​01)≫ε⁡(α1​…​αj​0)\displaystyle\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...10)\!\gg\!\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...1)\!\gg\!...\!\gg\!\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}01)\!\gg\!\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}0) (18)

for any binary “prefix” α1​…​αi​0\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}0 such that the word α1​…​αj​011​…​10\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...10 above has at most n+1n+1 letters107107 107 The reason the conditions (18) allow us to address the definition of ε~​(α​1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha 1) for all the binary words of interest (i.e., all the words that end with an “1”) is the following: (i)(i) we only need to define ε~​(α​1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha 1) for words α​1\alpha 1 of length nn or less; and (i​i)(ii) the word “α1​…​αj​0\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}0” above is allowed to be the empty word, in which case we replace “ε⁡(α1​…​αj​0)\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}0)” by “0” above (this lets us cover the case of ε~​(11​…​1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(11...1) for words “11…1” of length from 1 to nn)..

Moreover, the same inequalities can be summarized in an even simpler way108108 108 A useful difference between (19) and (18) is that in the set of inequalities (19) each ε~​(α1​…​αj​011​…​1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...1) appears only once., as

ε⁡(α1​…​αj​011​…​10)≫ε~​(α1​…​αj​011​…​1)≫…≫ε~​(α1​…​αj​01)≫ε⁡(α1​…​αj​0)\displaystyle\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...10)\!\gg\!\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...1)\!\gg\!...\!\gg\!\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}01)\!\gg\!\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}0) (19)

for any binary “prefix” α1​…​αi​0\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}0 such that the word α1​…​αj​011​…​10\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...10 above has exactly n+1n+1 letters109109 109 This is because we already know that, if a word of the form α1​…​αj​011​…​110\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...110 has a longer sequence of 1’s (denoted “11…11”) than the shorter word α1​…​αj​011​…​10\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...10, then we have ε⁡(α1​…​αj​011​…​110)≫ε⁡(α1​…​αj​011​…​10)\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...110)\!\gg\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...10)..

We will now show that the inequalities (19) can be simultaneously satisfied. Indeed, recall how in the previous section we defined110110 110 Recall that in the previous section, when discussing nn-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprints, at first we only considered ε⁡(α)\varepsilon(\alpha) for binary words α\alpha that ended in a zero; but then it became convenient to define ε⁡(α)\varepsilon(\alpha) for all binary words α\alpha of length exactly nn (with the exception of the word “11…1”).

ε⁡(α1​…​αi​011​…​11):=ε⁡(α1​…​αi​0),\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}011...11):=\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}0),

where we obtained the word α1​…​αi​011​…​11\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}011...11 by adding a sufficient number of 1’s at the end of the word α1​…​αi​0\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}0 to make it have maximal length (which was nn in our discussion in the previous section, but it is n+1n+1 here). Our plan now is to try to use a similar idea111111 111 But now we do this “in opposite direction”, i.e., now we try to extend the definition to the shorter words by using the fact that we already have a definition for the longest words; in the previous section its was the other way around. in order to define ε~​(α1​…​αi​1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}1) for words that end with “1”; we will see that this almost  solves the problem raised by the inequalities (19), and then we will make one more adjustment in order to solve it fully.

Indeed, let us first (temporarily) define

ε~​(α1​…​αi​1):=ε⁡(α1​…​αi​111​…​11),\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}1):=\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}111...11),

where, like above, we added a sufficient number of 1’s at the end of the word α1​…​αi​1\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}1 to make it have length n+1n+1.

Then, if we check the inequalities (19), we will see that they are “almost” satisfied, except we actually have

ε~​(α1​…​αi​11)=ε~​(α1​…​αi​1),\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}11)=\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}1),

because when we add a sufficient number of 1’s at the end of the word α1​…​αi​11\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}11, and also add a sufficient number of 1’s at the end of the word α1​…​αi​1\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{i}1, we actually obtain the same word of length n+1n+1. Therefore, instead of (19) we actually have

ε⁡(α1​…​αj​011​…​10)≫ε~​(α1​…​αj​011​…​1)=…=ε~​(α1​…​αj​01)=ε⁡(α1​…​αj​0),\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...10)\gg\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...1)=...=\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}01)=\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}0),

where the word “α1​…​αj​011​…​10\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...10” has exactly n+1n+1 letters, and the common prefix “α1​…​αj​0\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}0” may also be the empty word, in which case we replace ε⁡(α1​…​αj​0)\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}0) by “0”.

Then, since “there is enough space” between the order of magnitude of ε⁡(α1​…​αj​011​…​10)\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...10) and the order of magnitude of ε⁡(α1​…​αj​0)\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}0), we can now modify all the values ε~​(α1​…​αj​01),…,ε~​(α1​…​αj​011​…​1)\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}01),...,\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...1) to impose that we have

ε⁡(α1​…​αj​011​…​10)≫ε~​(α1​…​αj​011​…​1)≫…≫ε~​(α1​…​αj​01)≫ε⁡(α1​…​αj​0),\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...10)\gg\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}011...1)\gg...\gg\tilde{\varepsilon}(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}01)\gg\varepsilon(\alpha_{1}...\alpha_{j}0),

and we obtain a solution for the inequalities (19).

8 Proof of the global attractor conjecture in the nn-dimensional case

Consider some toric dynamical system 𝐓n{\bf T}_{n} in ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}. As we discussed in previous sections, we embed 𝐓n{\bf T}_{n} into a toric differential inclusion 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n}, and we already know that, if we can construct an exhaustive family of ZSH for 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n}, then we obtain a proof of the global attractor conjecture.

We know that we can construct a ZSH blueprint ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} for 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n}. After that, our plan is the following: (Step 1) explain how to convert ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} into the kind of “restricted ZSH blueprint” denoted ℬnP\mathcal{B}_{n}^{P}, whose tiles are contained in the set 𝒟nP\mathcal{D}_{n}^{P}, such that ℬnP\mathcal{B}_{n}^{P} can be used for the construction of ZSH117117 117 Recall that, when we used a ZSH blueprint ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} to construct ZSH in 3D, the blueprint ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} was restricted to the set 𝒟2P\mathcal{D}_{2}^{P}, or equivalently, was restricted to the set 𝒟2H\mathcal{D}_{2}^{H}. for 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n}, and (Step 2) explain how we can use ℬnP\mathcal{B}_{n}^{P} for the construction of an exhaustive family of ZSH for 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n}. We now discuss these two steps, in this order.

Step 1. Recall that, when we constructed a (say, two-dimensional) ZSH blueprint ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} in section 7, we did not restrict its tiles to the set 𝒟2P\mathcal{D}_{2}^{P}, which (up to identifying ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} with the affine plane {X1=1}\{X_{1}=1\} of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}) was the compactification of the set

{(X2P,X3P)∈ℝ2|1≤X2P≤X3P},\{(X_{2}^{P},X_{3}^{P})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}|1\leq X_{2}^{P}\leq X_{3}^{P}\},

but when we discussed two-dimensional ZSH blueprints in Section 6 (where we actually used these blueprint to construct two-dimensional polyhedral ZSH), all the tiles of a ZSH blueprint were contained inside 𝒟2P\mathcal{D}_{2}^{P} (for example, see Figure 4 (b)(b)).

Note though that the boundary rays of 𝒟2P\mathcal{D}_{2}^{P} are faces of the subdivision ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}. Then there is a very simple way to convert an already constructed ZSH blueprint ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} that is defined on the whole ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} (for an x1x_{1}-x2x_{2}-subdivision 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} that contains the faces of a given subdivision subdivision ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P} of 𝒟2P\mathcal{D}_{2}^{P}), into a “restricted ZSH blueprint” ℬ2P\mathcal{B}_{2}^{P} whose tiles are contained in 𝒟2P\mathcal{D}_{2}^{P}: for each tile T2T_{2} of ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} whose interior intersects 𝒟2P\mathcal{D}_{2}^{P} we define a tile T2PT_{2}^{P} of ℬ2P\mathcal{B}_{2}^{P} given by

T2P=T2∩𝒟2P.T_{2}^{P}=T_{2}\cap\mathcal{D}_{2}^{P}.

Also, we define the basepoint of T2PT_{2}^{P} to be the same as the basepoint of T2T_{2}. Note that, since the two boundary rays of 𝒟2P\mathcal{D}_{2}^{P} are union of faces of the subdivision ℱ2P\mathcal{F}_{2}^{P}, it follows that if a tile T2PT_{2}^{P} intersects the boundary of 𝒟2P\mathcal{D}_{2}^{P} then the basepoint of T2PT_{2}^{P} lies on the boundary of 𝒟2P\mathcal{D}_{2}^{P} (see Figure 4, Figure 9, and Figure 14 for examples.).

Also, in order to obtain exactly the kind of two-dimensional ZSH blueprint that we have used in Section 6, we need to also intersect all the tiles T2PT_{2}^{P} with a “blue box” of the form

[0,M3]×[0,M2],[0,M_{3}]\times[0,M_{2}],

for M3≫M2≫1M_{3}\gg M_{2}\gg 1, to obtain all the bounded tiles of ℬ2P\mathcal{B}_{2}^{P}118118 118 We also need to make sure that the horizontal side of the blue box (i.e., the side where we have {X3=M3}\{X_{3}=M_{3}\}) is a union of horizontal sides of tiles of ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2}, and the vertical side of the blue box (i.e., the side where we have {X2=M2}\{X_{2}=M_{2}\}) is a union of vertical sides of tiles of ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2}. In general, for the latter condition, we need to lengthen or shorten some (horizontal) sides for tiles of ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2}..

Finally, in order to finish the construction of ℬ2P\mathcal{B}_{2}^{P}, we need to construct the “boundary tiles” of ℬ2P\mathcal{B}_{2}^{P} (see Figure 10(a)(a)). For this, we choose tile vertices ViV_{i} along the sides of the blue box where we have {X3=M3}\{X_{3}=M_{3}\} or {X2=M2}\{X_{2}=M_{2}\}, in such a way that, when we draw rays that connect the origin to each ViV_{i}, the rays separate the slopes of rays contained within the subdivision 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2}119119 119 In other words, if two rays that are contained in 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} have the same slope, then the parts of those rays that are outside the big blue box are contained in the same boundary tile of ℬ2P\mathcal{B}_{2}^{P}..

The two-dimensional case discussed above suggests the following process for the transition from our construction of a “global” ZSH blueprint ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n} to the definition of a “restricted” ZSH blueprint denoted ℬnP\mathcal{B}_{n}^{P}, in any dimension. Let us start from the beginning, with the (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional fan ℱn+1\mathcal{F}_{n+1}120120 120 For ease of notation, let us say that our toric differential inclusion of interest is (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional, instead of nn-dimensional. Then, as we discussed in previous sections, without loss of generality we can assume that ℱn+1\mathcal{F}_{n+1} is x1x_{1}-x2x_{2}-…-xn+1x_{n+1}-symmetric, and contains all the hyperplanes of the form {Xi=Xj}\{X_{i}=X_{j}\} and {Xi=0}\{X_{i}=0\}.

In particular, ℱn+1\mathcal{F}_{n+1} gives rise to a “restricted fan” ℱn+1≤\mathcal{F}_{n+1}^{\leq}, whose cones are just those cones of ℱn+1\mathcal{F}_{n+1} that are contained within the set121121 121 If we are given ℱn+1≤\mathcal{F}_{n+1}^{\leq}, then, due to symmetry, we can reconstruct all the cones of ℱn+1\mathcal{F}_{n+1} that are contained in the closure of the negative orthant.

Remark. Recall that the Persistence Conjecture says that any nn-dimensional weakly reversible system is persistent [3]. A stronger version of this conjecture (called the Extended Persistence Conjecture [3]) says that any variable-kk weakly reversible system is persistent. We obtain the following partial result for the (Extended) Persistence Conjecture: any bounded trajectory of a variable-kk weakly reversible126126 126 Or, more generally, variable-kk endotactic system, because variable-kk endotactic systems can also be embedded into toric differential inclusions, see [33]. system is persistent.

9 Appendix: some general results about fans, toric differential inclusions, and ZSH

In this section we discuss some technical results that we used in previous sections. For some of these results, for the sake of a simpler notation, we formulate and prove them in 3D instead of nD; the proof in nD is analogous.

9.1 Finer and coarser fans, embeddings of toric differential inclusions, forward invariant regions

The following definition clarifies what we mean by “the fan ℱ1\mathcal{F}_{1} is coarser than the fan ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2}”, or equivalently, “the fan ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} is finer than the fan ℱ1\mathcal{F}_{1}”.

Definition 9.1.

Given two fans ℱ1\mathcal{F}_{1} and ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, we say that ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} is finer than ℱ1\mathcal{F}_{1} (or ℱ1\mathcal{F}_{1} is coarser than ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2}) if any cone in ℱ1\mathcal{F}_{1} can be written as a union of cones in ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2}.

We now want to show that forward invariant regions of toric differential inclusions generated by the finer fan are also forward invariant regions of toric differential inclusions generated by the coarser fan; for this we need the notion of “embedding” for differential inclusions.

Definition 9.2.

Given two differential inclusions d​𝐱d​t∈F1​(𝐱)\frac{d{\mathbf{x}}}{dt}\in F_{1}({\mathbf{x}}) and d​𝐱d​t∈F2​(𝐱)\frac{d{\mathbf{x}}}{dt}\in F_{2}({\mathbf{x}}), we say that the first one is embedded in the second one if F1​(𝐱)⊆F2​(𝐱)F_{1}({\mathbf{x}})\subseteq F_{2}({\mathbf{x}}) for all 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}.

The following lemma and its corollary allow us to replace a toric differential inclusion 𝒯1\mathcal{T}_{1} with a more convenient one (denoted 𝒯2\mathcal{T}_{2}) and argue that ZSH for the new toric differential inclusion are actually also ZSH for the old toric differential inclusion we started with.

Lemma 9.3.

Consider a number δ>0\delta>0 and two fans ℱ1\mathcal{F}_{1} and ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} such that ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} is finer than ℱ1\mathcal{F}_{1}. If 𝒯1\mathcal{T}_{1} is the toric differential inclusion generated by (ℱ1,δ)(\mathcal{F}_{1},\delta), and 𝒯2\mathcal{T}_{2} is the toric differential inclusion generated by (ℱ2,δ)(\mathcal{F}_{2},\delta), then 𝒯1\mathcal{T}_{1} is embedded in 𝒯2\mathcal{T}_{2}.

Proof.

Consider some 𝐱∈ℝ>0n{\bf x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0}. For each cone K1∈ℱ1K_{1}\in\mathcal{F}_{1} at distance <δ<\delta from the point log⁡(𝐱)\log({\bf x}), there exists some cone K2∈ℱ2K_{2}\in\mathcal{F}_{2} that is also at distance <δ<\delta from the point log⁡(𝐱)\log({\bf x}), such that K2⊆K1K_{2}\subseteq K_{1}. But this implies that the polars of these two cones satisfy K1o⊆K2oK_{1}^{o}\subseteq K_{2}^{o}, so we obtain

Fℱ1,δ​(log⁡(𝐱))⊆Fℱ2,δ​(log⁡(𝐱)),F_{\mathcal{F}_{1},\delta}(\log({\bf x}))\subseteq F_{\mathcal{F}_{2},\delta}(\log({\bf x})),

i.e., 𝒯1\mathcal{T}_{1} is embedded in 𝒯2\mathcal{T}_{2}. ∎

Lemma 9.3 immediately implies the following result.

Corollary 9.4.

Consider a number δ>0\delta>0 and two fans ℱ1\mathcal{F}_{1} and ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} such that ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2} is finer than ℱ1\mathcal{F}_{1}. Denote by 𝒯1\mathcal{T}_{1} the toric differential inclusion generated by (ℱ1,δ)(\mathcal{F}_{1},\delta), and by 𝒯2\mathcal{T}_{2} the toric differential inclusion generated by (ℱ2,δ)(\mathcal{F}_{2},\delta). Assume that 𝒯2\mathcal{T}_{2} cannot cross some surface 𝒵\mathcal{Z} within a set Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then 𝒯1\mathcal{T}_{1} also cannot cross 𝒵\mathcal{Z} within Ω\Omega.

9.2 Necessary and sufficient conditions for ZSH

Consider a ZSH denoted 𝒵\mathcal{Z} inside the unit cube (0,1)3(0,1)^{3}, and recall that we can assume that the normal line at any smooth point of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is contained in the union of the (closed) positive orthant and the (closed) negative orthant. The outer normal of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} at a point 𝐱∈𝒵\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{Z} is defined as the normal direction of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} at 𝐱\mathbf{x} pointing into the (closed) negative orthant. Then we have:

Lemma 9.5.

Consider a toric differential inclusion 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} in ℝ>03\mathbb{R}^{3}_{>0} with polyhedral fan ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} and assume that a piecewise smooth surface 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is a ZSH for 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} and is contained in the unit cube (0,1)3(0,1)^{3}. Then, for any point 𝐱∈𝒵\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{Z} where 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is smooth we have: if 𝒞∈ℱ3\mathcal{C}\in\mathcal{F}_{3} is a polyhedral cone such that log⁡(𝐱)∈𝒞\log(\mathbf{x})\in\mathcal{C}, then the outer normal vector of the surface 𝒵\mathcal{Z} at the point 𝐱\mathbf{x} must belong to the cone 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Proof.

Since 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is a zero-separating surface for 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} and log⁡(𝐱)∈𝒞\log(\mathbf{x})\in\mathcal{C}, it follows that the tangent plane to 𝒵\mathcal{Z} at 𝐱\mathbf{x} is a supporting plane of the polar cone 𝒞o\mathcal{C}^{o} (otherwise the cone 𝒞o\mathcal{C}^{o} would provide a way for trajectories of 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} to “cross through” the zero-separating surface 𝒵\mathcal{Z} at 𝐱\mathbf{x}). Therefore, the outer normal of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} at 𝐱\mathbf{x} must belong to the polar cone of 𝒞o\mathcal{C}^{o}. In conclusion, the outer normal of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} at 𝐱\mathbf{x} belongs to the polar of the polar of the cone 𝒞\mathcal{C}, which is simply 𝒞\mathcal{C}. ∎

Remark 9.6.

Lemma 9.5 provides a very convenient necessary condition that any ZSH 𝒵\mathcal{Z} should satisfy: its outer normal direction at any (smooth) point 𝐱\mathbf{x} must belong to a cone of ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} that is easy to specify, because it is exactly the cone that contains the point log⁡(𝐱)\log(\mathbf{x}). If several cones 𝒞∈ℱ3\mathcal{C}\in\mathcal{F}_{3} contain the point log⁡(𝐱)\log(\mathbf{x}), then we obtain more information from this lemma if we select the smallest such cone. Most importantly for us, this lemma provides a geometric condition for 𝒵\mathcal{Z} that does not involve polar cones any more; it only involves cones from the polyhedral fan ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3}.

We will see below that this necessary condition can be modified to obtain a very useful sufficient condition.

Lemma 9.7.

Consider a toric differential inclusion 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} in ℝ>03\mathbb{R}^{3}_{>0} given by a fan127127 127 Recall that we are assuming that our fans are x1x_{1}-x2x_{2}-x3x_{3}-symmetric and contain the planes xi=xjx_{i}=x_{j} and xi=0x_{i}=0. ℱ3\mathcal{F}_{3} and a fixed number δ>0\delta>0. Assume that for any cone 𝒞∈ℱ3≤\mathcal{C}\in\mathcal{F}_{3}^{\leq} we are able to specify a cone K𝒞⊂{X3≤X2≤X1≤0}K_{\mathcal{C}}\subset\{X_{3}\leq X_{2}\leq X_{1}\leq 0\} such that 𝒞\mathcal{C} is contained in the relative interior of K𝒞K_{\mathcal{C}} with respect to the set {X3≤X2≤X1≤0}\{X_{3}\leq X_{2}\leq X_{1}\leq 0\}, and the property below is satisfied:

For any ε^>0\hat{\varepsilon}>0 there exists a piecewise smooth surface 𝒵ε^\mathcal{Z}_{\hat{\varepsilon}} such that

(i)(i) 𝒵ε^⊂(0,1)3∖(ε^+[0,1]3)\mathcal{Z}_{\hat{\varepsilon}}\subset(0,1)^{3}\setminus(\hat{\varepsilon}+[0,1]^{3})

and

(i​i)(ii) for any smooth point P∈𝒵ε^P\in\mathcal{Z}_{\hat{\varepsilon}} we have: if log⁡(P)∈K𝒞\log(P)\in K_{\mathcal{C}}, then there is a normal vector n→P\vec{n}_{P} of 𝒵ε^\mathcal{Z}_{\hat{\varepsilon}} at PP such that128128 128 We will refer to this n→P\vec{n}_{P} as “the outer normal” of 𝒵ε^\mathcal{Z}_{\hat{\varepsilon}} at PP. Note that n→P\vec{n}_{P} belongs to the (closed) negative orthant of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. n→P∈𝒞\vec{n}_{P}\in\mathcal{C}.

Then, for any ε^\hat{\varepsilon} small enough, 𝒯3\mathcal{T}_{3} cannot cross 𝒵ε^\mathcal{Z}_{\hat{\varepsilon}} within (0,1)3(0,1)^{3}.

Proof.

Consider some 𝒞∈ℱ3≤\mathcal{C}\in\mathcal{F}_{3}^{\leq}. We need to show that for any ε^\hat{\varepsilon} small enough the following is true: if a point P∈𝒵ε^P\in\mathcal{Z}_{\hat{\varepsilon}} satisfies

log⁡(P)∈B⁡(𝒞,δ),\log(P)\in B(\mathcal{C},\delta),

where B⁡(𝒞,δ)B(\mathcal{C},\delta) is defined as the set of points at distance at most δ\delta from 𝒞\mathcal{C}, then there exists a normal vector of 𝒵ε^\mathcal{Z}_{\hat{\varepsilon}} at PP that belongs to 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Note first the following remark: for any cones 𝒞1,𝒞2⊂ℝn\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{2}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} such that 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} is contained in the interior of 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2}, it follows that there exists some number M>0M>0 such that we have

B⁡(𝒞1,δ)∖B⁡(0,M)⊂𝒞2,B(\mathcal{C}_{1},\delta)\setminus B(0,M)\subset\mathcal{C}_{2},

A short proof of this fact follows from the observation that dist⁡(𝒞1∩B⁡(0,1),∂𝒞2)>0\mathrm{dist}(\mathcal{C}_{1}\cap B(0,1),\partial\mathcal{C}_{2})>0, which implies that dist⁡(𝒞1∩B⁡(0,M),∂𝒞2)>δ\mathrm{dist}(\mathcal{C}_{1}\cap B(0,M),\partial\mathcal{C}_{2})>\delta for large enough MM.

Then we can apply the remark above to conclude that there exists some number M𝒞>0M_{\mathcal{C}}>0 such that we have

Finally, if ε^\hat{\varepsilon} is small enough, it follows that log⁡(P)\log(P) lies outside the ball B⁡(0,M𝒞)B(0,M_{\mathcal{C}}), and therefore log⁡(P)∈K𝒞s​y​m\log(P)\in K_{\mathcal{C}}^{sym}; but we also have log(P)∈{X3≤X2≤X1≤0}\log(P)\in\{X_{3}\leq X_{2}\leq X_{1}\leq 0\}, which implies log⁡(P)∈K𝒞\log(P)\in K_{\mathcal{C}}. Then the outer normal n→P\vec{n}_{P} of 𝒵ε^\mathcal{Z}_{\hat{\varepsilon}} at PP satisfies n→P∈𝒞\vec{n}_{P}\in\mathcal{C}. Now the desired conclusion follows from the fact that there are only finitely many cones 𝒞∈ℱ3\mathcal{C}\in\mathcal{F}_{3}, so for ε^\hat{\varepsilon} small enough we can guarantee that the reasoning above works for all 𝒞∈ℱ3≤\mathcal{C}\in\mathcal{F}_{3}^{\leq}. ∎

Remark 9.8.

Lemma 9.7 is very useful for our process for constructing the ZSH, because it allows us to “trade” the restriction that ε\varepsilon is very small (which we need to make anyway) to account for the possibility that δ\delta might be quite large. More specifically, in practice, it follows that it is sufficient to construct a single “good” ZSH blueprint, and the same blueprint will work for any (fixed) δ\delta; for larger δ\delta we just need to start the construction of the ZSH (for the same ZSH blueprint) with a smaller ε\varepsilon.

9.3 Restrictions of Ψ3P\Psi_{3}^{P}, and images of straight line segments via Ψ3P\Psi_{3}^{P}

Consider the function Ψ3P:(0,1)3→ℝ>02\Psi_{3}^{P}:(0,1)^{3}\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{2} given by

Ψ3P​(x,y,z)=(l​o​g​(x)l​o​g​(z),l​o​g​(y)l​o​g​(z)).\Psi_{3}^{P}(x,y,z)=\left(\frac{log(x)}{log(z)},\frac{log(y)}{log(z)}\right).

We show that if we restrict Ψ3P\Psi_{3}^{P} to an affine planes near the origin, and if this affine plane “cuts off” the corner of the positive orthant, then the restriction is a diffeomorphism:

Lemma 9.9.

Consider an affine plane π\pi that intersects the positive orthant and has a normal vector inside the negative orthant. If the distance between the origin and π\pi is small enough, then the restriction of

Ψ3P​(x1,x2,x3)=(log⁡x2log⁡x1,log⁡x3log⁡x1)\Psi_{3}^{P}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})=\left(\frac{\log x_{2}}{\log x_{1}},\frac{\log x_{3}}{\log x_{1}}\right)

to π\pi, i.e., the map

Ψ3P|π∩ℝ>03:π∩ℝ>03→ℝ2,{\Psi_{3}^{P}\Big|}_{\pi\cap\mathbb{R}^{3}_{>0}}:\pi\cap\mathbb{R}^{3}_{>0}\to\mathbb{R}^{2},

is a diffeomorphism between π∩ℝ>03\pi\cap\mathbb{R}^{3}_{>0} and its image via Ψ3P\Psi_{3}^{P}.

Proof.

We just need to check that the restricted map is injective and that it is locally a diffeomorphism (i.e., its Jacobian is not singular anywhere). These can both be verified using elementary calculations. For example, injectivity follows if we write the plane as

a1​x1+a2​x2+a3​x3=b,a_{1}x_{1}+a_{2}x_{2}+a_{3}x_{3}=b,

for some ai≥0a_{i}\geq 0 (not all zero) and some b>0b>0, and note that for any u,v>0u,v>0 the curve t→(t,tu,tv)t\to(t,t^{u},t^{v}) intersects this plane for at most (and actually exactly) one value t0∈(0,1)t_{0}\in(0,1). This also shows that we can allow the normal vector to lie on the boundary of the negative orthant, as long as we further restrict the domain to be the set π∩(0,1)3\pi\cap(0,1)^{3}. Also, we don’t even need the hypothesis that π\pi is very close to the origin; it is actually sufficient that π∩(0,1)3≠∅\pi\cap(0,1)^{3}\neq\emptyset. ∎

9.4 Asymptotic level sets of the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function

Consider a Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function V:ℝ>0n→ℝV:\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} given by

V⁡(x1,…,xn)=∑i=1n(xi​log⁡xixi0−xi+xi0),V(x_{1},...,x_{n})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i}\log\frac{x_{i}}{x_{i}^{0}}-x_{i}+x_{i}^{0}),

for some fixed (x10,…,xn0)∈ℝ>0n(x_{1}^{0},...,x_{n}^{0})\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}. Then we have:

Lemma 9.11.

For large values of MM, the level set of the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function given by the equation

V⁡(x1,…,xn)=M,V(x_{1},...,x_{n})=M,

is contained between two simplicial sets of the form

∑i=1nxi=α⁡(1±Clog⁡M)\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}=\alpha\left(1\pm\frac{C}{\log M}\right)

for some value α∼M/l​o​g​(M)\alpha\sim M/log(M) and for some for some constant C>0C>0 that depends only on nn.

Proof.

The proof of this lemma follows from elementary considerations. For example we can calculate the minimum of VV and the maximum of VV along an arbitrary simplex of the form ∑i=1nxi=α.\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}=\alpha. for large values of α\alpha. (The minimum is attained at a point xm​i​nx_{min} that is proportional with the vector x0x_{0} that shows up in the expression of VV, and the maximum is attained at a point xm​a​xx_{max} where all but one of the coordinates are zero; the nonzero coordinate of xm​a​xx_{max} is the one where x0x_{0} has its smallest coordinate.) ∎
